- **Three colours, and `down` means customers.** At four metres a person distinguishes three reliably. `down` is reserved for a sev1 incident or a probe that is down; everything else that is wrong is `degraded`, because the screen's job is to make somebody walk over rather than to grade the problem for them.
- **Rotation is derived from the wall clock, not a local timer** (`rotationIndex(now, panels, seconds)`). Two televisions in one room rotating out of step is the sort of thing people notice and nobody can explain, and a browser that was asleep resumes in the right place instead of continuing from where it stopped. An empty panel is never rotated to — a wall that spends a third of its time showing an empty heading trains a room to stop looking at it.
- **`unknown` is not `down`.** A probe that has never run has not failed; putting it on the wall as a failure would make a freshly created probe look like an outage.
- **Sync health comes from `paging_incidents`, not from a column on the account** — that is the signal the org already gets woken up by, and a wall that disagreed with the pager about whether an account is broken would be worse than no wall.
- **A source belongs on the wall only once the table it reads exists.** The wallboard shipped with a query-monitors source reading `query_monitors` with raw SQL, ahead of that feature's migration, on the theory that the absence would be tolerated — but a guard cannot tell a missing table from a broken query, so every screen sat permanently amber with "Could not read: query monitors" on it, which is the exact failure the amber rule exists to prevent, caused by the rule itself. The source was removed and came back with the feature, as an ordinary schema-typed read. `server-core/src/__tests__/wallboard-feed.test.ts` pins what the wall says when a source fails.
- **Session-authenticated on purpose.** Unlike the iCalendar feed and public status pages, this carries incident titles, probe names and account names, and a screen in an office is exactly what a visitor photographs. The machine driving the wall signs in once.
- **`refreshSeconds` / `rotateSeconds` are clamped, not validated.** A wallboard URL gets typed into a television with a remote control; a 400 there is a black screen nobody can debug.
- **Deliberate omissions.** No kiosk token (see above). No dashboard rotation — a dashboard is a sitting-down artefact, and putting one on a wall is what this feature exists _instead of_. No mobile surface.

Docs: `website/src/content/docs/features/wallboard.md`.

## Operations calendar (cloud-only)

One time axis over six things the org already stores. API **1.28.0**; migration `0115_ops_calendar` adds exactly one table, and it is not for events.

- **Nothing on the calendar is a record.** Freezes, sleep windows, expiry-feed deadlines (which already merge plugin-declared fields with resource leases), commitment term ends, cron-triggered workflows and declared incidents are all projected on read, the posture/backup-coverage stance: a calendar event has no identity of its own, and materialising one would create a second thing that can be stale. Ending a freeze early therefore stops it on the calendar _at the moment it was ended_ (`updatedAt` for an inactive row), not at the date it was declared to run to — which is the one place the projection deliberately disagrees with the stored column.
- **The one table is `calendar_subscriptions`**, and it exists because a URL somebody pasted into Google Calendar eighteen months ago has to keep working, be attributable and be revocable. Token hashed with plain SHA-256 — right _here and only here_: it is 32 bytes from `randomBytes`, so there is no low-entropy guess space for a KDF's work factor to defend, and the lookup sits on a route a hundred phones may poll. `user_id` is `set null` on delete: a feed that vanished because someone offboarded is how a team loses its shared calendar.
- **`GET /api/calendar/{token}.ics` is registered outside every auth layer**, beside the public status pages and for the same reason — a calendar client can hold no session. Two consequences are deliberate: the URL carries **no org id** (a leaked feed must not become a way to learn one and start probing org-scoped routes), and the feed carries scheduling facts only, never a credential, a cost or a resource id. Unknown and revoked tokens get the same 404, because the difference is exactly what someone probing tokens wants to learn.
- **`overlapsWindow`'s null means a _point_, not an open end.** A deadline with `end: null` in the past overlaps nothing; a freeze held until further notice overlaps every future window. The two readings both matter, so span sources pass `RUNS_FOREVER` (`Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`) rather than letting the shape of the value decide — the first cut read a null end as a point and silently dropped every open-ended freeze that began before the month being viewed.
- **Day bucketing walks date strings, not instants.** Stepping an instant by 24 hours skips a date every spring-forward (23:30 UTC on the 26th and 27th are both late evening in London; on the 28th it is already 00:30 on the 29th) and repeats one every autumn. `groupCalendarEventsByDay` resolves the two endpoints with `Intl` and counts calendar days between them.
- **Sources fail independently.** `listCalendarEvents` runs them under `allSettled` and reports `failedKinds` on the wire; the section renders a named degradation. A summary surface that silently drops a source is worse than one that says it did — the `CostsPanel` four-section call.
- **The section owns the window**, unlike every other section (host fetches, section renders): the month is a control on the page, and lifting it into two hosts would mean writing the same month arithmetic twice. `onRangeChange` is held in a ref so the fetch fires on a window change and not on a parent re-render, and both panels discard out-of-order responses by request number — paging quickly through months is exactly how a stale month lands on top of a newer one.
- **`buildIcsCalendar` lives in client-core** because RFC 5545 fails in ways only a unit test catches: octet-counted folding at 75 (a character-counted fold splits a multi-byte character into bytes no parser can decode), backslash escaped before the separators, CRLF throughout (clients that reject bare LF do it by rendering an empty calendar), and an all-day event needing `VALUE=DATE` with an _exclusive_ next-day `DTEND`. UIDs come from the event's stable id — a UID that changes per render makes every refresh a delete-and-recreate, which subscribers see as duplicates.
- **Surfaces**: `ui/src/calendar/CalendarSection.tsx` (month grid, agenda, subscriptions), web `WebCalendarPanel`, desktop `DesktopCalendarPanel` (cloud-only, with the Backups sign-in message — five of the six sources are org state a local workspace cannot hold). Reads take `resources:read`; subscriptions take `org:settings:write`, the API-key stance, because minting an unauthenticated URL over the org's schedule is an org-wide decision.
- **Deliberate omissions.** No mobile surface yet (a month grid is the one view a 6-inch screen argues with, and the agenda half duplicates the Expiring screen it already has), no CLI subcommand, and no Terraform resource — a subscription's whole value is a secret returned once, which is not something a state file should hold.

Docs: `website/src/content/docs/features/ops-calendar.md`.

## Runbooks (cloud-only)

The org's procedures, made runnable, plus the record of who did what. API **1.33.0**; migration `0117_runbooks` adds three tables.

- **A run is a snapshot, not a pointer.** Starting one copies every step's title and kind into `runbook_run_steps`, and the runbook's name onto the run. A postmortem that renders today's wording against last month's run is not merely stale — it is quietly wrong about what somebody was asked to do. This is the whole reason the run's steps are a table rather than a jsonb column.
- **The second reason is concurrency, and it is the load-bearing one.** Two responders working the same incident tick different steps at the same moment; a read-modify-write of a shared jsonb loses whichever lands second. Per-step rows make each tick an independent `UPDATE`, so the failure mode cannot occur. The runbook's _own_ steps stay jsonb because they are only ever read and written whole, by one editor — a workflow's `source` exactly.
- **Three step kinds, deliberately not a scripting language.** A runbook is written by whoever is on call for whoever is on call next, and the moment it needs a language it stops being written. `workflow` is the escape hatch, and it **records** which workflow run was started rather than starting one: the run goes through the workflow routes with their own permission, approvals and secrets, because a second execution path behind a weaker gate is how the first gate stops mattering.
- **Two permission levels, and the split is the feature.** Reading _and performing_ take `resources:read` — a checklist nobody on call can open is worse than no checklist, and requiring an admin to tick a box mid-incident is how a team stops using it. Editing takes `org:settings:write`.
- **Closing a run does not settle its outstanding steps**, and reopening is not offered. A run completed with three steps pending says the incident ended before the checklist did, which is the one thing a postmortem wants to know; and a record that can be edited after the fact is not a record. `runbookProgress` counts skipped as settled but not as done, so 100% cannot be reached by skipping everything.
- **`incident_id` on a run is a plain column, not a cascading FK.** Deleting an incident must not delete the evidence that somebody followed the failover procedure at 03:14. The runbook link _does_ cascade, because deleting a runbook is an explicit "this procedure is gone" — and `enabled: false` exists precisely so nobody has to.
- **The name conflict comes from the unique index, not a pre-check.** Check-then-insert loses the race, and the race here is two people writing up the same incident afterwards. `asNameConflict` turns the violation into the message the user needs.
- **A patch is validated after merging**, so a patch that only changes the steps still has to leave a runbook that is valid as a whole — the `updateBackupPolicy` stance. A step sent with its `id` keeps its identity, which is what lets a run in progress still match it.
- **`normalizeRunbookSteps` drops the reference belonging to the other kind.** A step switched from link to workflow that kept its URL would render a button pointing somewhere nobody meant. Link URLs are `https:` only — `javascript:` is the obvious attack and plain `http:` is barred too, because the one thing a runbook link reliably points at is an internal console.
- **Surfaces**: `ui/src/runbooks/RunbooksSection.tsx` (list + editor + runs), web `WebRunbooksPanel`, desktop `DesktopRunbooksPanel` (cloud-only, with the Backups sign-in message — a runbook is a shared document and a run is a record of who did what, both org state).
- **Deliberate omissions.** No resource-detail tab yet, though `runbookMatchesResource` and the stored selector already answer "which runbooks apply here" — only the surface is missing. No SSH-snippet step kind (fan-out targeting is a surface of its own). No mobile surface, no CLI subcommand, no Terraform resource yet.

Docs: `website/src/content/docs/features/runbooks.md`.

## On-call rotations (cloud-only)

Who to wake, rather than which channel to shout into. API **1.34.0**; migration `0118_on_call_rotations` adds three tables and one new member on the `AlertDestination` union.

- **The feature is one destination kind.** `{ kind: "on-call", scheduleId }` resolves to a person at delivery time, so a rule reading "database alerts -> whoever is on call" survives Monday's handover with no edit. Everything else here exists to answer that resolve.
- **Shift arithmetic is calendar-day arithmetic in the rotation's zone, never 24-hour arithmetic.** A rotation stepped in fixed milliseconds drifts an hour at each DST change until the 09:00 Monday handover happens at 08:00 — or until the boundary lands on the wrong side of the handover and two people each think the other is on call. `resolveOnCall` counts calendar days from `startDate` and resolves the handover instant with `wallTimeToUtc`, the same two-pass `Intl` helper the sleep schedules use. There is a test that pins 09:00 local across the British autumn transition.
- **The day a shift belongs to is decided by the handover time, not by midnight.** At 08:00 on handover Monday, last week's shift is still running.
- **A resolve that finds nobody is not an error.** Disabled, empty, not yet started, or a failed read all return null, the destination contributes nobody, and the rule's _other_ destinations still deliver. `resolveOnCallNow` catches and logs rather than throwing, because it sits on the alert delivery path and an alert lost to a misconfigured rotation is strictly worse than one delivered without its on-call leg.
- **Participants are a table, not a jsonb list, and the reason is deletion.** A rotation naming somebody who left the org pages nobody, silently, on their week; only `ON DELETE CASCADE` on the user FK makes removing them from the org remove them from the rotation. Same for covers.
- **Covers are stored, not folded into the rotation.** "Sam covered Tuesday night" is a fact somebody reads back six months later, and a rotation edited to express a one-off is a rotation nobody can reason about. Overlapping covers resolve **most-recently-started wins**, so row order never decides who gets woken up.
- **Escalation walks the rotation, never a cover** (`nextOnCall`). A cover is somebody standing in for one shift; escalating to "whoever is covering next Tuesday" is not what an escalation means. It returns null for a one-person rotation, and the caller falls back to the rule's own escalation destinations.
- **Delivery dedupes by _user_, not by schedule.** Two rules naming two rotations that happen to have the same person on call this week must not ring their phone twice. The on-call leg counts one _person_ as one destination, matching the way `push` counts as one however many devices it reaches.
- **The on-call push still respects the member's own mutes** (`sendPushToOrgUser` applies the same per-trigger filter as the org fan-out). An org rule decides whether the org is told; a member decides whether their phone rings, and being on call is not a licence to bypass that.
- **Permissions split three ways, and the middle one is the interesting one.** Reading is `team:read` (nobody should have to ask an admin who is on call); editing a rotation is `org:settings:write`; **arranging cover is `team:read`**, because it happens at 17:55 on a Friday and the person handing over is rarely an admin — with every cover audit-logged, which is what makes the looser permission safe.
- **Surfaces**: `ui/src/settings/OnCallSection.tsx` (Settings, beside Notifications — the rules that consume a rotation live there). The shift preview is fetched from the server rather than computed locally, so it cannot disagree with who actually gets woken up. `AlertRulesResponse` gained `onCallSchedules` (live rotations only, the disconnected-Slack-install rule) so the routing editor and the CLI can render a rotation by name.
- **The Terraform provider mirrors both halves**: `infrawrench_on_call_schedule` for the rotation, and a `schedule_id` on an `infrawrench_alert_routing` destination whose `kind` is `on-call`. Covers are deliberately not a resource — they are decided the morning somebody wakes up ill, and a plan that reverted one would be actively harmful.
- **Deliberate omissions.** No per-rotation escalation policy separate from the rule's own, no round-robin across rotations, no SMS/phone leg for the on-call destination (Twilio paging is org-wide), no mobile surface. `next` is already on the wire, so the escalation half is one step away.

Docs: `website/src/content/docs/features/on-call.md`.

## Paging providers (PagerDuty, incident.io; cloud-only)

The paging integration is a **generic plugin capability**, not two integrations. `plugin-base/src/paging.ts` defines `manifest.paging` (target label, whether acknowledge can be sent as an event, optional `onCall`/`incidents`/`webhook` halves) and optional client methods (`listPagingTargets`, `sendPagingEvent`, `listPagingOnCallSources`, `resolvePagingOnCall`, `listPagingIncidents`, `getPagingIncident`, `updatePagingIncident`, `registerPagingWebhook`, `removePagingWebhook`) plus `Plugin.verifyPagingWebhook` (on the Plugin because it needs only the secret). `server-core/src/paging/providers.ts` is the only consumer and has no provider name in it; the contract tests check that a declared half has its methods. Migration `0146_paging_providers`: `paging_provider_settings`, `paging_provider_events`, `paging_provider_incidents`.

- **Two destination kinds.** `{kind:"paging-provider", accountId, targetId}` opens an upstream alert; `{kind:"provider-on-call", accountId, sourceId}` resolves people through the plugin, maps them to members by lowercased email and joins the `on-call` leg's per-user set (one push per person across both). The target id is the provider's own; the plugin looks up the routing key or source token itself, so a rule never holds a secret.
- **`AlertEvent.lifecycle` is what makes it two-way.** `{key, phase: "open"|"acknowledged"|"resolved"}` with a stable key per condition: `probe:<id>`, `metric-alert:<rule>:<resource>`, `incident:<id>` (mitigated = acknowledged), `sync:<account>:<type>`, `page:<source>:<key>`, `workflow-page:<workflow>:<key>`. A non-open phase is applied by `routeAlert` to **every** upstream alert that key opened, before and regardless of rule evaluation (a recovery must close the incident the outage opened even if the rules changed), and never opens a new one. `clearExternalPage`/`clearWorkflowPage`/`closeOpenIncident` call `applyPagingLifecycle` directly because clearing raises no alert; `closeOpenIncident` only does so when it actually closed a row, since it runs on every successful poll. Alerts without a lifecycle get `<trigger>:<resourceId|key|account|title>`, so a re-raise re-triggers the open upstream alert instead of opening another.
- **Dedup key** is `iw:<orgId>:<lifecycleKey>` (`pagingDedupKey`, client-core), readable on purpose and trimmed to PagerDuty's 255.
- **One row per upstream alert doubles as the outbox.** `paging_provider_events` is unique on (account, target, dedup key); `pending_action` + `next_attempt_at` are the queue, claimed with the lease-in-the-due-column idiom. A send is tried inline only where `pluginCodeAvailable()` (false in the web edge Worker, whose plugin functions are stubs) and the `paging-providers` **gateway** pass retries with 2^n-minute backoff up to 8 attempts; a 4xx other than 408/429 is given up on at once and shown with `Gave up:`. After a send, the row's current `state` decides whether a follow-up is queued (a resolve that arrived mid-trigger is not lost). A resolve on a row whose trigger never reached the provider just settles it (nobody was paged). Acknowledge on a provider without `supportsAcknowledgeEvent` (incident.io HTTP sources) records the state without a send.
- **Acknowledgements go both ways.** `acknowledgeAlert` (Slack button, web) calls `acknowledgePagingForDelivery`, which acknowledges every upstream alert carrying that `alert_delivery_id` (written when the leg armed an escalation row). Upstream acknowledgement or resolution, from a webhook or the reconcile, runs `settleFromUpstream`: it moves the event row without echoing it back and settles the matching `alert_deliveries` row with the same `state = 'awaiting_ack'` conditional update `acknowledgeAlert` uses, `acknowledged_via = <pluginId>`, the member matched by email when the provider names one. `alert_delivery_id` has no FK (satellite schema; it is a pointer the sync matches on).
- **Provider on-call on the web edge** cannot run plugin code inline, so `routeAlert` splits those destinations into a leg held until "now"; the edge-runtime `alert-follow-up` pass (the poller Worker has real plugins) releases it within a tick. `holdUntil === now` is exempt from `bypassQuietHours`.
- **Inbound** is opt-in per account (`inboundEnabled`). Webhooks are nudges: `/api/paging-webhooks/:token` (public, gateway-routed, 1 MB cap) finds the settings row by an unguessable token, decrypts the secret (AAD `paging-provider/<account>/webhook-secret`), has the plugin verify, then re-reads each named incident through `getPagingIncident` (at most 20 per delivery) because payloads arrive out of order. Managed webhooks (PagerDuty) are subscribed on enable and removed on disable; manual ones (incident.io has no webhook API) store a pasted secret. The reconcile runs every 2 minutes without a webhook and every 15 with one, window = last sync minus 10 minutes. Turning inbound off deletes the mirror. Retention: resolved events and incidents older than 30 days are pruned by the same pass.
- **Naming.** Three "incidents" now exist: provider _status_ incidents (`status-incidents`, `infrawrench incidents`), _declared_ incidents (`incidents`, `infrawrench declared-incidents`) and _pager_ incidents (`paging-incidents`, `PagerIncidentRecord`, `infrawrench paging`). Never shorten the third to "incidents".
- **Surfaces.** Routing editor: `PagingDestinationsField` in `DestinationPicker` (a select per account, not a checkbox wall: PagerDuty accounts have hundreds of services), fed by `GET /paging-providers/destinations`, loaded separately so a slow provider never holds the rules up. Settings: `PagingProvidersPanel` at the bottom of the On-call section (mirroring toggle, webhook URL + secret, sync now, who is on call upstream, recent outbound events). Incidents tab: `PagerIncidentsList` above the declared list via optional `IncidentsClient.listPagerIncidents`/`actOnPagerIncident` (desktop IPC `cloud_paging_incidents_list`/`_act`; the settings allowlist gained `paging-providers`). Mobile: the same list with Acknowledge/Resolve on the Incidents screen; no notification action buttons (mobile has no notification-category pattern yet). CLI: `infrawrench paging [--all] | ack|resolve <ref> | events`, and `routing` renders the new kinds. Terraform: `paging-provider`/`provider-on-call` destination kinds (`account_id`, `target_id`, `source_id`) and `infrawrench_paging_provider_settings` (write-only `webhook_secret`; schemas listed in `schemasKnownAbsent` until the spec is regenerated). Not exposed as MCP or chat tools.
- **Permissions**: configuration `org:settings:write`; acknowledge/resolve `incidents:write` (written upstream as the session's email; PagerDuty falls back to the account's default `From` user); upstream on-call preview `team:read`.

## Restore drills (cloud-only, a fourth tab on Backups)

Backup coverage answers "is there a backup"; drills answer "does it restore, and how long does it take". API **1.36.0**; migration `0120_restore_drills` adds one table.

- **It records, it does not restore.** Restoring a customer's database unattended costs real money, can collide with production, and cannot be generically verified — so the product will not do it. What it can do is make the exercise scheduled, recorded and visible when it lapses, which is the part organisations actually fail at. Every design decision below follows from that.
- **Only `verified` counts as evidence.** A restore that produced a running system nobody looked inside (`restored-unverified`) is exactly how a team discovers mid-incident that the dump had been empty for months. It is stored, because doing the restore is worth recording, and it does **not** reset the clock — `drillStanding` reports such a resource as `never`.
- **A later failure outranks an earlier success.** Somebody tried more recently than the last green tick and it did not work; reporting the resource as verified because March went well is the reading that gets a team hurt. The last success is still reported alongside, so the page can say when it was.
- **A `verified` drill must carry the measured RTO, and a `blocked` drill must not.** The RPO comes from the backup and the RTO can only come from somebody with a stopwatch — that number is the entire point. A blocked drill never started, so a duration is meaningless, and a meaningless RTO on this page is the most dangerous number on it. Enforced in `validateRestoreDrill`, normalized again in the store, and constrained in SQL — three places agreeing is cheap next to one place being the only thing between a made-up number and the summary that averages it.
- **The summary's RTOs come from currently-_verified_ rows only.** A measurement from a drill that has since gone stale is a number about a system that has changed underneath it. `worstRtoMinutes` is null rather than zero when nothing is verified.
- **`performed_at` is not `created_at`.** People write these up on Monday for a drill they ran on Saturday, and every staleness computation uses the performed date. `drillStanding` sorts rather than assuming input order for the same reason.
- **`resource_id` carries no foreign key**, deliberately. A drill is evidence about a _system_, not about a row: it must survive the resource being re-synced under a new internal id, and it must certainly survive somebody deleting the resource, because "we tested this and then removed it" is a fact an auditor asks about. Those orphans are reported in `orphanedDrills` rather than dropped.
- **The eligible population is `protected` or `automated` coverage rows.** A resource with no backup cannot be drilled, and listing it here as "never tested" would duplicate the coverage page's own unprotected finding while burying the ones that genuinely can be tested.
- **Recording takes `resources:write`, not `org:settings:write`.** Recording a drill is reporting what you did, not changing what the org demands, and the person who spent Saturday restoring a database is rarely the person who set the objective. Deletion is audited: removing evidence that a restore failed is exactly the edit a reviewer wants to see.
- **Surfaces**: a fourth tab on the existing `BackupsSection` rather than a new workspace tab — drills are that screen's missing half, and a separate page would let somebody read the coverage without ever seeing that none of it has been tested. Fetched as a third request rather than folded into the coverage payload, because the standings are computed _over_ the coverage and folding them in would make every caller of `/backups` pay for them.
- **Deliberate omissions.** No scheduled reminder yet (the standings go stale visibly; a `drillAlerts` routing trigger is the obvious next step). No mobile surface. No CLI subcommand.

Docs: the Drills section of `website/src/content/docs/features/backup-coverage.md`.

## Query monitors (cloud-only)

A read-only SQL query on a schedule, with a threshold and an alert. API **1.37.0**; migration `0121_query_monitors` adds one table.

- **It exists because metric alerts watch the provider, not the data.** The orders table that stopped growing, the dead-letter queue with 4,000 rows, the ETL that wrote nought — each is one query and no metric.
- **The read-only guard is an allowlist of leading keywords, and it runs on every execution rather than only on save.** A monitor executes unattended, on a schedule, with the account's credentials, forever, which is a categorically different risk from the SQL editor where a person watches a statement run — so the check is a property of the _stored query at execution time_, not of the person who saved it. A denylist was rejected outright: it must be right about every dialect's spelling of every destructive verb, forever, and only has to be wrong once. `normalizeMonitorSql` strips comments first (`-- harmless\nDROP TABLE x` starts with a comment), and the single-statement rule catches `SELECT 1; DROP TABLE users` — which the leading-keyword check alone would wave through. Semicolons inside string literals are not statement separators.
- **`unknown` is a first-class state.** A monitor whose query failed has not told you the data is fine; rendering that as `ok` is how a broken monitor becomes indistinguishable from a healthy one, which would defeat the feature. It is styled neutrally rather than red, because unknown is _broken_, not _breaching_, and the driver's own message is passed through — "relation does not exist" is the single most useful thing this feature can say.
- **A failure does not reset the breach streak.** Breach, error, breach is two breaches; treating the error as a recovery would let an intermittently failing query hold off an alert forever.
- **The alert fires on the run that _reaches_ the streak, not on every run past it.** `>` would never fire and `>=` would page every interval until somebody fixed it; `=== consecutiveBreaches` fires exactly once per episode, and an `ok` run re-arms it.
- **Editing the query, mode, operator or threshold re-arms the monitor** (streak to 0, state to `unknown`). The stored streak was accumulated against a different question, and carrying it forward would fire on the first run of a rule nobody has tested.
- **`runMonitorQuery` lives in server-core, not in the web route**, and mirrors the SQL editor's connection paths (`client.executeQuery`, per-resource driver, SQL peer integration, account-level driver) so a monitor can watch anything the editor can query — and so the poller, which has no HTTP context, runs exactly the same resolution.
- **The editor's target picker is fed by `GET /query-monitors/targets`** (API 1.39.0), because the resource-scoped path shipped with no way to select a resource — a database that is a _resource_ (ClickHouse service, D1, Turso, Databricks warehouse) simply could not be monitored from the UI, and the desktop panel passed no account options at all, so desktop could not create monitors, full stop. `listQueryMonitorTargets` derives the list from **static plugin metadata** rather than instantiated clients: `manifest.sqlDriver` marks an account-level target, and a resource qualifies when its type declares `resourceSqlDriver` **or `supportsRestQuery`** — a new plugin-base flag for REST-queried types (`executeQuery` is a plugin-wide client method, so BigQuery datasets and Spanner databases had nothing static to find them by; set it on any new type of that shape or the picker will not offer it). Accounts with neither are omitted entirely. Create/update validate `resourceId` against the synced rows (org- and account-ownership) and take the row's `resourceTypeId` as authoritative, so API callers may omit the type; the editor keeps a monitor's stored target selectable even when the picker no longer offers it, so editing never silently reassigns the query. `server-core/src/__tests__/query-monitor-targets.test.ts` pins the shipped database types against the real registry.
- **A resource also qualifies through a SQL peer integration** (`sqlPeerIntegrationsOf` in the same store): a type whose `peerIntegrations` map an output onto the `credentialKey` of a plugin whose `manifest.sqlDriver` names a driver this host ships. That is how every managed database that has no driver of its own is queryable — Neon projects/branches/databases, PlanetScale branches, RDS instances and clusters, Redshift, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Azure SQL/Flexible, DO/OVH/Scaleway managed databases — and the first shipped picker missed the whole class (Neon was the report). The per-resource gates the peer tabs honour apply here too: `showWhen`/`requiresFields` filter against the synced row's fields (an engine-gated DO cluster running Valkey is not offered), and `unreachableWhen` both hides the target and, at run time, surfaces the provider's guidance title as the failure. Execution resolves the peer's credentials through `buildPeerPluginClient` (rewriters included) and runs the peer's account-level driver, passing `caCertKey` when the mapping carries a CA (DO's own CA would otherwise fail TLS verification).
- **The poller claim pushes `next_run_at` forward _before_ running.** Run-then-reschedule means a monitor whose query hangs until the process dies is claimed again immediately by the next replica, and a slow query becomes a stampede against the customer's own database. The batch is small and runs **sequentially**: every monitor opens a connection to somebody else's production.
- **Permissions follow the SQL editor.** Reading is `resources:read`; creating, editing and test-running are `resources:execute`. The audit entry records the query text — a scheduled statement against a customer database is exactly what an audit reader wants to see, and the guard means it can only ever be a read.
- **Alerts route through the org's rules** under the existing `metricAlerts` trigger rather than a new one, so a monitor can reach a channel, a phone or whoever is on call without this module knowing any of that exists.
- **The wallboard's fourth source ships here**, in the change that creates the table it reads — see the wallboard section for why that is a rule and not a preference. Both states that are not `ok` go on the wall: breaching, with the value against the threshold, and `unknown`-after-a-failed-run, with the driver's message, because a wall that renders a monitor nobody can run as green is the same lie the state exists to prevent. A monitor that has never run is on neither, the rule the probes already follow. There is no `since` on those lines — a monitor keeps its last outcome, not a history, and a duration derived from the streak would put a number on the wall that nothing backs.
- **Deliberate omissions.** No stored run history — a monitor's value over time is a metric and the product already has a place for metrics; a second, worse time series here would be a table nobody prunes. No per-monitor alert routing (that is what routing rules are). No mobile surface. Desktop is cloud-only for a reason beyond org state: the schedule runs in the poller, so a local monitor would only run while the app was open.

Docs: `website/src/content/docs/features/query-monitors.md`.

## Carbon estimate

Estimated operational CO2e beside every price. API **1.42.0**; **no migration**: a read over synced inventory, plugin declarations and a static coefficient table. The org view is cloud-only; per-resource and create-form figures also work in desktop local mode.

- **Anything that cannot be placed gets no number.** Region absent from the coefficient tables, or no vCPU count: each produces an `unestimated` row with a reason and contributes nothing. A carbon figure computed against a guessed grid is worse than no figure, because it is a number somebody will put in a report. The count of unestimatable rows (`unestimatedCount`, since the list is capped) sits _beside the total_, because a total covering two thirds of an estate reads exactly like a complete answer. Reason order is provider (grid table) before region before size, so an unsupported grid never sends somebody hunting a region mapping.
- **Plugins declare how to read; client-core holds every number.** `ResourceTypeDefinition.carbon` (`CarbonDeclaration` in plugin-base): `regionFieldKey`, `grid` (defaults to the plugin id; `"auto"` tries AWS, GCP, Azure in turn, for Kubernetes nodes and `aws-us-east-1`-style prefixed regions), optional `gridFieldKey`, `vcpus` (`{ from: "field", format?: "k8s-quantity" }` or `{ from: "size", catalogueTypeId?, catalogueFieldKey?, matchBy?: "label", stripPrefix?, stripSuffix?, list? }`), `countFieldKey`/`countOffset`, and `role`. A type with only `rightsizing` is read through it (`effectiveCarbonDeclaration`), so a plugin that gains right-sizing gains carbon. A type with neither is **out of scope**, not unestimated: a bucket must not inflate the "could not be estimated" count. Size resolution goes through the create form's size-picker (RDS/ElastiCache/OpenSearch/MSK/MQ borrow EC2's catalogue with their `db.`/`cache.`/`.search` affixes stripped; OVH's picker ids are per-region UUIDs, so it matches by label).
- **`role: "aggregate"` is how double counting is avoided.** Managed clusters (EKS, GKE, AKS, DOKS, Kapsule, OVH MKS) are shown on their page and in their create form but never summed: their nodes are listed as instances in their own right. Kubernetes nodes are `instance`, but `getCarbonEstimate` skips a node whose name (or the IP encoded in an EKS `ip-a-b-c-d` name) matches an instance row's name, external id or `privateIp` output, and reports the number as `duplicateCount`.
- **Coefficients (`client-core/src/carbon-factors.ts`) have two bases, and every row says which (`gridBasis`).** `ccf`: Cloud Carbon Footprint's AWS/GCP/Azure per-region tables, reproduced verbatim (quirks included) from its April 2026 HEAD by evaluating its constants files, not by hand. `ember-2024`: Ember 2024 lifecycle country figures (via OWID's dataset) for every other provider, mapped from where the datacentre physically is (`PROVIDER_REGION_ZONES`; DO `nyc1`/`nyc3` are in New Jersey, `nyc2` in Manhattan has no figure and is left out). US sites outside the hyperscaler tables use CCF's NERC-region figures so Ashburn reads the same grid for every provider. Azure regions CCF lacks are filled from Ember rather than CCF's "unknown" average, which this module never uses. A test asserts every figure lands in 1–1100 g/kWh: a unit slip is a three-orders-of-magnitude error that looks reasonable in a table. Grid figures are location-based, not market-based.
- **PUE and watts.** CCF's per-provider watts (code values, not the methodology page, which lags); providers CCF lacks reuse its AWS average, as CCF does for Alibaba. PUE: CCF's hyperscaler figures (GCP per region where published), Hetzner 1.13 for its own parks, OVHcloud 1.24 (FY25 group), Scaleway per availability zone from its environmental-footprint reference, and the Uptime Institute 2025 average 1.54 (`COLOCATION_PUE`) for DigitalOcean, Fly and Hetzner's colocated ash/hil/sin.
- **Utilisation is a constant, and it is on the wire.** 50%, the upstream default and the largest single source of error. A figure derived from the few providers that report CPU history would be quietly inconsistent across an estate.
- **One formula, every surface.** `estimateFootprint` is the only place the arithmetic lives. Surfaces: the Costs panel section (web, desktop via `cloud_carbon_estimate`, mobile `CarbonSection`); `carbon` on the `POST /resources/cost-estimate` response (detail header `CarbonEstimateChip`, edit-modal delta, mobile resource card, CLI `estimate`); the create form, computed **locally** by `estimateCreateFormCarbon` from the size-picker's vCPUs and the region field, using a `carbon` hint the host (never the plugin) attaches to `CreateResourceConfig` (`carbonHintFor` on the server, `createCarbonHint` in desktop local mode), with each `SizeCard` reading `CreateCarbonContext`; right-sizing's `currentMonthlyKgCo2e`/`monthlyKgCo2eSaving` (`carbonSaving`); the environment-template estimate's `monthlyKgCo2e`; MCP/chat `get_carbon_estimate` and `estimate_resource_footprint`; CLI `infrawrench carbon`; workflow `infra.carbon.estimate/resource` (cloud-only, `costs:read` in `WORKFLOW_OPERATION_PERMISSIONS`); custom-graph `graph.carbon.estimate`. Web and desktop dedupe the in-flight `cost-estimate` request so price and carbon cost one round trip.
- **`server-core/src/cost/carbon.ts` owns the reads**, not web: the environment estimate and workflow runner need them too. Create configs (the size catalogues) are cached per (org, account, type) for an hour, so a detail view does not cost a provider round trip each time; a failed catalogue costs its resources an estimate (`unknown-size`), never the report.
- **`costs:read` for the org figure.** It is a reporting figure that sits beside spend and ends up in a board pack. A single resource's figure rides the cost-estimate route's `resources:read`, like its price.
- **Fly machines are read from the `cpus` field** the lister syncs from `config.guest`; a machine with no guest config has no `cpus` and reads as an unknown size.
- **Deliberate omissions.** No storage, memory or egress estimate (the coefficients exist but the inventory does not carry volumes reliably); no GPU estimate (DO dedicated inference, Fireworks, Together sync GPU counts but no region-placed GPU model the CCF table can use consistently); no AI-API token emissions (only vendor per-prompt disclosures exist, not per-token figures); no embodied emissions; no Databricks clusters (no synced region, and on classic compute they are the cloud account's VMs anyway); no per-resource time series; no weekly-digest line yet; Vultr and Oracle have no plugin, so no table. Linode has one (2026-10, `linode` in `PROVIDER_REGION_ZONES`, colocation PUE) mapped from the city each region id names; Jakarta `id-cgk` is deliberately absent because Indonesia has no Ember figure in the table.

- **Deliberate omissions.** No storage, memory or egress estimate (the coefficients exist but the inventory does not carry volumes reliably); no GPU estimate (DO dedicated inference, Fireworks, Together sync GPU counts but no region-placed GPU model the CCF table can use consistently); no AI-API token emissions (only vendor per-prompt disclosures exist, not per-token figures); no embodied emissions; no Databricks clusters (no synced region, and on classic compute they are the cloud account's VMs anyway); no per-resource time series; no weekly-digest line yet; Vultr and Linode have no plugin, so no table. Oracle Cloud (`oracle-cloud` grid) maps OCI region ids to Ember countries / NERC regions; regions in a country Ember has no row for (South Korea, Switzerland, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Morocco, Ireland, Serbia) and Shawnee (SPP) are left out, and OCI publishes no PUE, so it reads `COLOCATION_PUE`.

Docs: `website/src/content/docs/features/carbon.md`.

## Pushing in from outside (pages & cost rows over the API)

Two endpoints let a server that isn't Infrawrench push _into_ it — the mirror image of everything else, which pulls. Both are the HTTP twin of a workflow primitive, and in both cases the workflow path was refactored to share the mechanism rather than being copied.

**Routing/auth.** `POST /api/org/:orgId/costs/rows` (`web/src/api/routes/cost-ingest.ts`) and `POST|DELETE /api/org/:orgId/pages` (`routes/pages.ts`) are registered on `api` **before** the `orgScoped` mount, exactly like chat, because `sessionMiddleware` 401s an `iwk_` key and an unattended caller has nothing else. They authenticate through `web/src/auth/org-request-auth.ts` `authenticateOrgRequest(c, pathOrgId, scope)` — session cookie / WorkOS bearer / API key, pinned to the path org, permission enforced on **every** path via `effectivePermissions` (so a key never exceeds its owner's role). That module is chat's old `chat/auth.ts` generalized; `authenticateChat` is now a four-line wrapper that only narrows the scope type. New permissions: `costs:write`, `pages:write` — deliberately **not** in the member system role.

**Cost push.** `server-core/src/cost/cost-ingest.ts` holds the validator/mapper/writer for every non-collected cost row; `cost/workflow-costs.ts` (`infra.costs.write`) and `cost/external-costs.ts` (the endpoint) are thin callers differing only in their `CostIngestSource` — plugin id, reserved tag, fallback account id, error prefix, per-call cap. The reserved tag is the whole invariant: `cost_daily`'s ORDER BY doesn't include `plugin_id` and is frozen, so pushed rows carry `infrawrench:workflow=<id>` or `infrawrench:source=<name>` to keep their key space disjoint from the pollers' and from each other. Ids live in db-free `cost/workflow-cost-ids.ts` / `cost/external-cost-ids.ts`; API rows report provider `external` and, absent an `accountId`, account `external:<source>`. `web/src/services/cost-query.ts` labels both synthetic providers in one `providerNames()` helper and now labels synthetic accounts in `labelSeries` too, not just in the dimension list.

**Paging.** `server-core/src/paging/deliver.ts` owns the protocol — resolve key/cooldown, claim, fan out over Twilio/push/Slack/Teams, roll the claim back when every transport reached nobody — behind a `PageCooldownStore` interface, because the cooldown row differs per caller but nothing else does. `workflows/paging.ts` backs it with `workflow_pages` (keyed by workflow); `paging/external-pages.ts` backs it with the new `external_pages` table (keyed by org+source+key, migration `0036`). Both claims are a single conditional upsert whose `setWhere` reads the existing row, which is what stops two replicas double-paging. API pages reuse the **`workflowPages` notification trigger** rather than adding a fourth column to three tables — the user-facing label across web/mobile is now just "Pages". Push payload gains an `api_page` variant (`client-core/src/push.ts` + `mobile/src/lib/push.ts` parse/route, deep-links to the org home).

`source` is one idea across both surfaces, so its rule lives once in `server-core/src/source-name.ts` (`isValidSourceName`, `SOURCE_NAME_HELP`).

**CLI.** `infrawrench page <message> --source …`, `infrawrench page clear`, and `infrawrench costs push --source … [--file|stdin]` (`desktop/electron/cli/commands/push.ts`) wrap both endpoints — the CLI is usually already on the box that has the news. Suppressed pages exit zero and print the retry time.

Docs: `website/src/content/docs/features/server-push.md` (+ cloud-costs, workflows, cli, push/Slack/Teams alert triggers, roles, api-keys).

## Org config as code (cloud-only)

One JSON document carrying everything an org configures that is neither a provider account nor a live resource: dashboards (with their cards), workflows, custom graphs, budgets, metric alert rules, synthetic probes, cost centres + allocation rules, the tag policy, and the five org-wide alert-settings rows. Export is a read fan-out; apply is the same writers in one transaction. Verb pair: `config export` / `config plan` / `config apply`.

- **Keys, not ids.** Every entity is addressed by a slug derived from its name (`uniqueOrgConfigKey`), never by a row id — that is what makes one document apply to a staging org, a fresh DR org, and the org it came from. Cross-references are rewritten on export and resolved on apply: a budget widget's `config.budgetId` becomes `budgetKey`, a `custom_graph` widget's `graphId` becomes `graphKey`, a workflow's budget trigger carries `budgetKey`, an allocation rule's `accountId` and the drift scope carry account **display names**. `client-core/src/org-config.ts` holds the document + plan types, the section→permission tables, `ORG_CONFIG_KEY_PATTERN`, and the key derivation; the zod schema lives in `web/src/services/org-config/schema.ts` with instantiated `Exact<>` assertions against those types (**instantiated** — a bare `type X = [Exact<A,B>]` alias resolves to `never` without erroring, so the existing `SchemasMatchCostContract`-style guards only bite when something assigns `true` to them).
- **Key derivation must run over a stable order.** `state.ts` orders every collection by `createdAt, id` — deliberately NOT the order the list endpoints use. `listWorkflows` sorts by `updatedAt`, so deriving keys from that would rename every key whenever someone saved a workflow, and the next apply would delete-and-recreate the lot.
- **One state loader for both directions.** `loadOrgConfigState(orgId)` returns each row already rendered in document shape, so export serialises it straight out and apply diffs the incoming document against it. A round trip is only lossless if "what we have" and "what a document says" are computed by the same code — which is also what makes an unchanged document report as entirely `unchanged` rather than rewriting everything.
- **Three verbs, `web/src/api/routes/org-config.ts`** — `GET /config/export` (`?sections=` narrows), `POST /config/plan` (the dry run; read-only, so a PR reviewer can run it), `POST /config/apply`. New permissions `config:read` / `config:write`, **plus** the per-section permission of every section involved — `config:write` alone would otherwise be a way around a role that deliberately withholds `workflows:write`, since a document carries workflow source. Export refuses rather than omitting a section the caller can't read: a partial document looks complete, and applying it with `replace` would delete everything the exporter couldn't see. Admin gets both through `ALL_EXCEPT`; Member gets neither.
- **Plan then execute.** `buildOrgConfigPlan` resolves every reference and queues closures (`(tx) => Promise<void>`) while nothing is written; ids for creates are minted during planning so later sections can point at them. `applyOrgConfig` then runs the whole queue inside one `db.transaction`. This is why the writes are direct `tx` calls rather than calls into `services/budgets.ts` et al — those helpers close over the module-level `db` and can't join a transaction. The validators are still shared (`budgetInputSchema`'s threshold/filter schemas, `widgetConfigSchemaFor`, `normalizeTagPolicy`, `normalizeAnomalySettings`, `normalizeProbeUrl`, `PROBE_LIMITS`, `METRIC_ALERT_LIMITS`, `DRIFT_ALERT_LIMITS`, `EXPIRY_ALERT_LIMITS`), so a config document can never smuggle in a shape the hand-editing route would refuse. `EXPIRY_ALERT_LIMITS` moved to `client-core/src/expiry.ts` and is re-exported from `server-core/expiry/settings.ts` in the process; `DRIFT_ALERT_LIMITS` already had a client-core copy.
- **`merge` vs `replace`.** Merge creates and updates what the document names. Replace additionally deletes what it doesn't — but only **within the sections the document carries**, so a budgets-only file can never touch workflows whichever mode it runs in. The default dashboard is never deleted (the hand-editing route refuses too); that shows up as an `unresolved` entry rather than a silent skip.
- **`unresolved` is not an error.** A resource pin nobody has synced, an account name this org hasn't connected, a workflow whose budget trigger names a budget the document doesn't define — each is reported and the affected card/clause/deletion is dropped, so a restore is not held hostage by one dangling pin. Two things fail loudly instead, because guessing is worse: a drift scope that resolves to zero accounts (empty means _every_ account, so dropping unknown names would widen alerting), and a widget/probe the normal editor would also have rejected.
- **What is deliberately out.** Accounts and credentials (an export must never be a credential leak), resources, workflow webhook **signing** secrets (write-only by contract — the read path redacts them, so no document can carry one), and every claim/bookkeeping column: `lastNotifiedAt`, `lastSentWeekStart`, `smsLastPagedAt`, firing history, run logs, change freezes. Restoring a cooldown claim from a `git push` would re-open a quiet period and page people twice. Enabling the digest through a document sets `lastSentWeekStart` to the current window, exactly as `updateOrgDigestSettings` does, so an apply can't fire a digest immediately.
- **Dashboard cards are anonymous and ordered**, so the only sound update is to replace the whole set — done only when the card list actually differs, so an unchanged document doesn't churn widget ids on every apply. Same rule for a cost centre's allocation rules. `gridX` is the index in the one sequence all three card tables share (see the dashboard card-order section above).
- **Surfaces** — CLI `infrawrench config export|plan|apply` (`desktop/electron/cli/commands/config.ts`; `--out`, `--sections`, `--prune`, `-y`; apply always plans first, even with `-y`, so an unattended run leaves a record of what it did, and refuses to apply unconfirmed on a non-TTY). Shared settings section `ui/src/settings/ConfigAsCodeSection.tsx` (registry key `config`, permission-gated on `config:read`) — the preview is not optional there either. Desktop reaches it through the existing `cloud_settings_request` allowlist (`config` added to the org alternation). **Mobile is a deliberate omission**, alongside the Monaco editors and the anomaly-tuning knobs: this is a git-workflow surface whose input is a file.
- OpenAPI `paths/org-config.ts`; API_VERSION 0.38.0 → **0.39.0**. Docs: `website/src/content/docs/features/config-as-code.md` (+ cli.md, roles-and-permissions.md).

### Bulk move and delete of reports and folders (API `1.47.0`)

`POST /cost-reports/bulk` (`costs:write`) takes `{action: "move", reportIds, folderIds, targetFolderId}` or `{action: "delete", reportIds, folderIds}`, at most 500 items, and is **all or nothing**: `web/src/services/cost-reports-bulk.ts` locks the org's folder rows and the named report rows `FOR UPDATE` inside one transaction, checks every item, and only then writes. Checks: exists and not soft-deleted; per-object sharing via `objectAccessProblem` (new, the non-throwing half of `requireObjectAccess`, against one resolver per type rather than one load per item): editor to move, `delete` semantics to delete; for a move, **editor on the destination folder**, because folder grants inherit to what is filed in it, so filing is a widening of access (the single-report PUT does not check this; a known asymmetry); and the tree rules against the tree _as it will be_ (`costReportBulkMoveBlockers` in client-core applies every move to a copy, then runs `costReportFolderMoveBlocker` per moved folder, so moving a parent and child together is fine and two folders that fit alone but not together are caught). An invisible item reads as "no longer exists", never as a 403, matching the single-item 404s. A refusal is a 400 with `problems: [{kind, id, name, message}]` and a message that **names the first three items itself**, because the desktop IPC bridge, the CLI and MCP keep only the message. Deletes restate `softDeleteCostReport`/`deleteCostReportFolder`'s effects inside the transaction (cards, schedules paused, sharing rows; folder contents fall to the top level by SET NULL). Audit is one row per item after commit (`cost_report.move`, `cost_report_folder.move`, `.delete`) with `bulk: true`.

UI (`ui/src/cost-reports/CostReportBulk.tsx` + `CostReportsPanel`): checkboxes only when the host wires `bulkUpdate`; shift-click ranges run over `costReportListOrder` (display order) and take the anchor's state; **Select contents** per folder; keyboard on the list section (Ctrl/Cmd+A, M, Delete, Esc; ignored inside text fields); drag a row or folder heading onto a folder heading or the **Folders** rail (only shown with folders and bulk). The drag payload lives in panel state, not `dataTransfer`, because `dragover` cannot read the data and that is when a target must decide whether to accept; refused targets never `preventDefault` and show why. CLI `reports move <item>... --folder <path|top>` and `reports delete <item>... [-y]` (one item per positional, `folder:` prefix for folders); MCP `bulk_move_cost_reports` / `bulk_delete_cost_reports`. Mobile is read-only for reports, so it has no bulk actions.

## IaC reconciliation — the ClickOps detector (cloud-only)

An org uploads the Terraform state it already has; every synced resource is classified **managed / drifted / unmanaged**, and the unmanaged ones become `import` blocks. `Plugin.terraformExport` was one-way (inventory → HCL); this is the inverse read.

**Naming, because there are now four.** Four features in this repo have "Terraform" in the name, and each entry below already had to disambiguate against the other three — so, once, in a table:

| Feature                | Direction               | Unit                | Where                                          |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| **IaC reconciliation** | Terraform state → in    | user's cloud rsrcs  | `client-core/src/iac/`, `server-core/src/iac/` |
| eject to Terraform     | HCL → out               | user's cloud rsrcs  | `plugin-base/terraform*.ts`                    |
| org config as code     | one JSON doc, both ways | the Infrawrench org | `web/src/services/org-config/`                 |
| Terraform provider     | Terraform → Infrawrench | the Infrawrench org | `terraform-provider-infrawrench/`              |

Call this one **IaC reconciliation** in prose and `iac` in code. It is the only one that reads state _in_. It shares the mappers with eject-to-Terraform and nothing at all with the other two.

- **The reverse mapping is derived, never written twice.** `client-core/src/iac/type-map.ts` `deriveTerraformTypeMap` probes each plugin's own `terraformExport.mapResource` with a `Proxy`-backed `fields` bag (four probe values — a string, `"1"`, `"true"`, `"[]"` — so mappers that branch on a value are covered, unioned) and reads the block type back. A plugin that gains export support gains reconciliation for free, and the two directions cannot drift apart. `ownKeys` on the proxy stays **empty** on purpose: a mapper that iterates the bag (tags, labels) must see nothing rather than an infinite set of invented keys. What cannot be derived — a mapper needing a field shape a probe can't fake — lands in `underivable` with a reason and is **shown in the UI**, because a silently missing type reads as "nothing maps to this" rather than "we couldn't tell". It only costs the _state→inventory_ direction: with a real resource in hand the real mapper runs, so matching still works.
- **Two document shapes, version-checked rather than assumed.** `client-core/src/iac/state.ts` reads a raw `.tfstate` (**format version 4** — `resources[].instances[].attributes`) and `terraform show -json` (**format_version 1.x** — `values.root_module`, recursing `child_modules[]`). Version 3 and version 5 are both refused with an explanation; a half-read state would report genuinely managed resources as ClickOps, which is exactly the wrong answer. A plan document (`planned_values`, no `values`) gets its own message. Every bound lives here because the input is untrusted: 8 MiB, 10 000 instances, 250 attributes each, 4 000 chars per value, **64 levels of nesting**, 50 000 nodes per measurement — each enforced _ahead of_ the work it guards (document size on the raw text before `JSON.parse`, via `TextEncoder` byte length rather than code units; the rest incrementally, short-circuiting), never by measuring the whole thing and asking afterwards. The depth bound is the one that is about _shape_ rather than volume, and it exists because the old size measurement was `JSON.stringify`, which recurses: a size-compliant document nesting ~20 000 deep overflowed the stack and escaped as a `RangeError`, i.e. an HTTP 500. `measureStructure` now walks an explicit stack, depth-first so a deep chain trips in as many steps as it is deep. Note V8's `JSON.parse` is _iterative_ and swallows such documents happily — only stringify blows up, so the bug lived entirely in the measurement.
- **Parse-failure translation is total, not an allow-list.** `saveIacState` turns **any** throw from the parse stage into a 400 (`TerraformStateParseError` keeps its message; anything else is logged as a parser gap and still answers 400 with a useful description). Matching on known error classes is precisely what let the `RangeError` through, and the status is not a detail here: a 500 says "we broke", which invites a blind retry of a file that will never work, where a 400 says "this document is not acceptable". Parsing is the trust boundary, so the translation belongs at the boundary rather than in a growing list of recognised types.
- **Secrets: the document is parsed and thrown away.** Only the projection is stored. `sensitive_attributes` (cty paths — the first `get_attr` step names the top-level key) and `sensitive_values` (a `true`-leaf mirror) are both honoured, and a nested sensitive leaf redacts the **whole** top-level attribute — half-redacted structures invite mistakes. Redacted keys survive as names in `redactedAttributeKeys` and are then **filtered out of the diff**, so a secret's value cannot leak through a drift row either. The audit entry for an upload carries counts, never values. **`redactedAttributeKeys` is "values we did not store", not "secrets"** — a clamped value (a truncated string, an oversized structure replaced by `IAC_OMITTED`) goes in the same list, because a value we changed is a value that must never be compared or the storage limit itself reads as drift. The two are counted apart (`redactedAttributeCount` = sensitive, `omittedAttributeCount` = too large) since only one of them is a thing to be careful with, and both are surfaced as parse warnings.
- **The drift comparison is `diffResourceRecords`** — the change-timeline differ, not a second implementation. The state attribute bag plays `prior`, the attributes the export mapper produces from live inventory play `fetched`; the differ walks the keys of the _incoming_ bag, which is exactly the set of attributes the mapper claims to know, so provider bookkeeping in a state entry produces no noise. `normalizeComparableValue` coerces numeric strings on both sides first (`"8"` vs `8` is not drift). The renderer is shared too: `ChangeDiffList` was split into `ResourceFieldDiffList({ diff })` + a thin `ChangeDiffList({ entry })` wrapper so both surfaces render one field diff one way.
- **Matching is identity-first and refuses coincidences.** Candidates in order: the mapper's `importId`, then `externalId`, then — only when the plugin gives no Terraform type — an `id`/`arn`/`self_link` that resolves to **exactly one** unconsumed state entry. Ambiguity is not a match. Every row reports `matchedBy` so the classification can be argued with. A matched resource no plugin can express is `managed` with an `unmappableReason` and counted in `summary.undiffable` — its drift is **unknown**, never reported as absent.
- **Four categories, not three.** Resources in state with no inventory match are their own list (`stateOnly`), split by whether any plugin maps that Terraform type at all — "your account isn't connected" and "nothing here maps `acme_widget`" are different problems.
- **The payoff is `import` blocks, generated by the existing pipeline.** `plugin-base/terraform-export.ts` gained `renderTerraformImportBlocks` + `exportResourcesForAdoption`; the document is Terraform 1.5+ `import {}` blocks followed by the stanzas `exportResourcesToTerraform` already produced. Declarative rather than N `terraform import` commands: the whole set comes under management in one reviewed apply.
- **The adoption invariant: a resource is declared only if it is also imported.** A stanza with no matching `import` block is a **create**, so a document advertised as "paste this and run `terraform plan`" that contains one either fails with already-exists or builds a second copy of a resource the user already has. `exportResourcesForAdoption` therefore drops any mapped resource whose plugin gave no `importId` and reports it in `unsupported` with `NO_IMPORT_ID_REASON` — the same "say so, don't guess" rule as `underivable`. This is why adoption is its own function rather than a renderer over a `TerraformExportOutcome`: the decision must happen **before** the bundle is rendered, so it re-exports the filtered set rather than post-processing (name deduplication is computed over the rendered set — a survivor must not keep a `_2` suffix it only needed to avoid a collision with something now absent). Plain eject-to-Terraform is unaffected: it declares without importing on purpose, and its comment hints are the right shape for reading one resource.
- **Attribution is the other half.** `server-core/src/iac/service.ts` joins `lookupResourceOwners` and the earliest `created` row in `resource_changes` (only `created` — an `updated` says somebody touched it, not that they made it), scoped to the **unmanaged** rows only, since that is the only place "who made this, and when" is a question. Two extra queries, not one per row.
- **Schema** `server-core/src/db/iac-schema.ts`, migration `0103_iac_reconciliation`: `iac_states` (org + optional account FK, both cascade; format/version/serial/lineage; parse warnings; uploader FK `set null`) and `iac_managed_resources` (state FK cascade, address/type/name/index key, `identifiers`, the redacted `attributes` bag). Retention rides the poller's hourly pass beside `pruneResourceChanges`: 20 documents per org on upload, 90 days after that — but `pruneIacStates` **always keeps the newest per org+account scope** (`DISTINCT ON`), because a quiet org must not silently lose its answer to "what does Terraform manage?".
- **API** `web/src/api/routes/iac.ts` — `GET|POST /iac/states`, `DELETE /iac/states/:id`, `GET /iac/reconciliation?stateId=`, `POST /iac/import-plan`, `GET /iac/resource?resourceId=` (a query param, because composite resource ids contain slashes — the `/changes/resource` rule). New permissions **`iac:read` / `iac:write`**: read is in the Member role for the same reason the change timeline is, write is not because uploading a state is the org declaring its estate. API_VERSION 1.10.0 → **1.15.0**.
- **Surfaces** — workspace-tab kind **`iac`**, title "IaC", full chain (ui.store union + three switches, `iacTabTarget`, both platforms' `lib/workspace-tabs.ts`, both viewports, two route stubs, desktop `validateWorkspaceTab` + web `validate-tabs` + the openapi `TabTarget` enum). Panel is shared: `ui/src/iac/IacPanel.tsx` + `IacImportPlanModal` behind a host-injected `IacClient` (web wraps `api*`, desktop wraps six new `cloud_iac_*` IPCs) — the `ChangesClient` arrangement. Desktop is cloud-gated in the panel, so a restored tab in local mode explains instead of fetching.
- **Deferred:** (the reverse direction now exists: GitHub issue filing maps a state scope to a repository to open IaC pull requests, see "GitHub issue filing and IaC pull requests") pulling state from a git repo through the existing GitHub App (the natural follow-up — this feature's input is a file today), a CLI subcommand, mobile, and the resource-detail badge's UI (the `GET /iac/resource` endpoint that backs it exists and is spec'd; nothing renders it yet).

## Terraform provider (`terraform-provider-infrawrench/`, standalone Go module)

Manages Infrawrench's **own** configuration as Terraform resources — 48 resources, 6 data sources, each with a per-object plan, drift detection and `terraform import`. Distinct from the three other "Terraform" features (see the naming table under "IaC reconciliation"): eject-to-Terraform writes HCL for the _user's cloud resources_, config-as-code moves a whole org as one JSON document, IaC reconciliation reads a user's Terraform state back in. This one is per-object CRUD against the org-scoped routes.

- **Why not wrap config as code.** That document addresses entities by a name-derived `key` with no server id, so `terraform import` is impossible and a rename plans destroy-and-recreate; apply is whole-document and transactional, which loses writes under Terraform's default parallelism of ten; and `replace` mode deletes anything the document doesn't name, so removing one budget would require owning every budget. It also carries only a handful of the object types the provider manages. Full argument in the provider README.
- **Two-file wire layer.** `internal/iw/wire.go` (cost allocation and reporting) + `wire_platform.go` (monitoring, governance, access, delivery) hold every struct; `endpoints.go` + `endpoints_platform.go` hold every typed method. **Nothing under `internal/provider/` assembles a URL or a body** — that package boundary is the invariant; the file split is readability. Hand-written rather than generated because the SDK generator collapses `discriminator` unions to `any` and drops `readOnly`/`default`, which are exactly the signals deciding whether a Terraform attribute is `Computed`.
- **Three omitempty conventions, and they are load-bearing.** A pointer _with_ `omitempty` means "omitted clears it" (most PUT full-replaces). A pointer _without_ means nil marshals as an explicit `null`, because the server distinguishes absent from null — cost centre `parentId`, account `bastionId`, metric-alert selectors. And where a route is a genuine PATCH (accounts, roles, Slack channels, Teams webhooks, deploy triggers) an omitted key means "leave alone", the opposite of the PUT case, so `Client.Patch` is kept visibly distinct from `Client.Put` rather than papered over.
- **Strict `oneOf` unions get custom marshallers.** `CostDateRange`, `CostExportDestination`, `AlertDestination` and `AlertCondition` are flattened into one Go struct each — that is what lets Terraform express them as a single repeatable block — with a `MarshalJSON` emitting only the named branch's keys. A push destination carrying a stray `channelId`, or a severity clause carrying an empty `values`, is a 400 rather than a field the server ignores. `wire_platform_test.go` pins each branch.
- **Objects with no single-GET route are read by listing and filtering**, and the wrapper synthesises the 404 itself so an out-of-band delete surfaces as "needs recreating" rather than silent success. That is most of them. **Bastions and API keys go further**: DELETE only _revokes_ and the listing keeps returning revoked rows, so `GetBastion`/`GetAPIKey` treat a non-null `revokedAt` as a 404 — without that, `terraform destroy` appears to succeed and the next refresh finds the object still there.
- **Org singletons destroy differently, on purpose.** `infrawrench_network_flow_settings` is the sharpest case: destroy turns collection **off**, because collection runs flow-log queries the provider bills to the customer's own cloud account and a no-op would keep spending their money for a resource they deleted. There is always exactly one settings row, so `Delete` cannot remove anything. Cost settings and alert routing **restore the shipped defaults** (an org routing nothing is worse than the default); currency **clears the display currency** but leaves the rate table; session recording is deliberately a **no-op** (silently disabling an audit control because a block was deleted is not a safe default); drift/expiry/posture are no-ops for lack of documented defaults. They import under the org id via `importOrgSingleton`.
- **Alert routing is one resource holding the whole ordered list**, not one per rule, because order _is_ the semantics (first-match-wins unless `continue_on_match`). Per-rule resources would have needed an invented position attribute and a way to stop two configs claiming a slot. Each rule's id is sent back on every write so in-flight held and escalating deliveries keep pointing at their rule.
- **Write-only fields are carried forward from prior state on every read** — account credentials, API key secret, SSH private key, bastion token, Teams webhook URL, Jira/Linear tokens, deploy answers. No route returns them, so a refresh that didn't carry them would empty them out of state. The provider cannot detect drift on any of them, and says so in each schema. `infrawrench_api_key`, generated `infrawrench_ssh_key` and `infrawrench_bastion` write a credential into state in plaintext because the API returns it once — documented as a state-backend warning rather than hidden.
- **Two client-side normalisations exist to stop permanent diffs.** `exchange_rate.rate` is a decimal string in a `numeric(20,10)` column, so `"1.085"` reads back `"1.0850000000"` — `sameDecimal` (a `big.Rat` compare) keeps the practitioner's spelling when the number is equal and takes the server's when it isn't. And a report notification writes back only the day field its cadence reads, since the server always returns both from non-null defaulted columns.
- **Three tests are the guard rails.** `wire_spec_test.go` fails when `openapi.json` describes a property no Go struct decodes and no `ignored` entry excuses (one-way; extra Go fields are expected because the spec lags). `provider_test.go` asserts `wantResources`/`wantDataSources`. `documentation_test.go` cross-checks the registry against the README table **and** `website/.../features/terraform-provider.md`, both directions — a resource nobody documented, or a table row for something removed, fails the build.
- **`schemasKnownAbsent` is empty** as of the 1.9.0 spec regeneration (which brought scenario models and billing rules in). The list and its test stay: the next object added ahead of a spec refresh goes there, and the test announces when the refresh catches up.
- **Adding a resource does not bump `API_VERSION`** — the provider is a client and changes no HTTP surface. Changing a route it calls does.
- **Outside every JS toolchain**, on purpose: not in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `turbo.json`, or `cliff.toml`'s `include_paths`. `cd terraform-provider-infrawrench && go build ./... && go test ./...`, Go 1.25+. `TF_ACC=1` adds acceptance tests, which need credentials and a scratch org.
- **API keys work; two resources are still closed to them.** `apiKeyOrgMiddleware` widened the org tree, so an `iwk_` key authenticates everywhere the provider reaches — except what `API_KEY_DENY_RULES` closes: `/api-keys` entirely and `/team` writes, i.e. `infrawrench_api_key` and writes to `infrawrench_role`. Those are acts a person performs (a key that mints keys outlives its own revocation; a key should not manufacture authority for others), so the provider explains the 403 rather than working around it — `apiKeyDeniedHint`, alongside `apiKeyUnauthorizedHint` for a 401, which now means the key itself was refused rather than the tree refusing keys. Adding a deny rule over a route the provider calls means updating both hints and the two schema descriptions.
- **Documented bounds are enforced bounds**, checked by `TestDocumentedRangesAreValidated`: it walks the served schema and fails on any attribute whose description states a range or length without a validator. Roughly 45 of them were unenforced before that test existed. Two flavours — most routes _reject_ out-of-range values (so validating converts a failed apply into a plan error), but the probe timings are _clamped_, where an unvalidated value applies fine and then disagrees with the configuration forever.
- **`docs/` is the Registry's documentation tab**, generated by `tfplugindocs` from the schemas and committed — the Registry reads it from the release tag and nowhere else, so a provider published without it renders "Documentation Unavailable" (which `v0.1.1` did). The generator is pinned as a Go tool dependency and CI regenerates and fails on a diff, so a schema change cannot ship documenting the previous version. `examples/` supplies the provider index example, per-resource `resource.tf` and an `import.sh` per resource; the directory is in `.prettierignore` because Prettier and the generator otherwise rewrite each other forever.
- **Two versions have been burnt to packaging**, which is why the publish workflow dry-runs the release before touching the satellite: `v0.1.0` attached the registry manifest without a checksum for it (`release.extra_files` does not feed the checksum step — it needs `checksum.extra_files` too), and `v0.1.1` shipped with no `docs/`. Both looked complete everywhere except at the Registry. `project_name` is also pinned in `.goreleaser.yml`: unpinned it defaults to the repo name, which is right in the satellite by luck and wrong anywhere else.
- **Published through a satellite repository**, `Infrawrench/terraform-provider-infrawrench`, on the SDK pattern: the Registry resolves to a Git URL and demands a dedicated repo named `terraform-provider-{NAME}`, which a monorepo subdirectory cannot satisfy. Monorepo is the direction of truth; the satellite's tree — including the `release.yml` that runs GoReleaser there — is mirrored wholesale from `terraform-provider-infrawrench/`, so nothing in it is hand-maintained. Release ritual is one edit to `VERSION`; the ledger is the monorepo tag `terraform-provider-v<version>`, written last so it means "handed off". The provider versions independently of `API_VERSION` — it is a client. MIT licensed rather than BUSL-1.1, because it is vendored into other people's infrastructure repos.

## Linux app server (`linux-appserver/`, standalone Rust workspace)

The remote half of Linux application support: a headless Wayland compositor that runs on a customer's host and streams **one application window per workspace tab** back to the desktop app and the web app. **Phase 1 as of Aug 2026** — protocol, encoder, launcher and the Smithay compositor all exist and are tested against real applications on a real VM; nothing in `app/` calls any of it yet. Verified end to end on Debian 13: GNOME Calculator and Firefox both render, and injected scroll input moves the page.

- **Why a compositor and not VNC.** A VNC server exports one framebuffer for a whole screen, so every window shares one tab and the tab bar carries no information. Per-window streaming needs something that _is_ the window manager. It also means the host needs nothing installed — no X server, no VNC server, no desktop environment, no `xpra` — which is the same call the embedded RDP client made: bundle the dependency, never shell out to whatever the host happens to have.
- **Four crates, split by whether they need Linux.** `iw-proto` (frame envelope, packed input, JSON control messages), `iw-codec` (damage coalescing, lossless encoder, tier selection), `iw-apps` (desktop entries, icon themes) and `iwappd` (session state machine, flow control, launcher, launch environment) all build and test on macOS. Only the `Backend` implementation behind `iwappd`'s trait seam is Smithay and Linux-only. Keeping that seam narrow is why ~137 tests run on a laptop instead of only in CI.
- **The encoder models the client's canvas, not the app's last frame.** `Encoder::prev` is what we believe the viewer holds, so rectangles whose pixels did not change are dropped (toolkits over-report damage constantly, and an idle window costs nothing). The consequence is a rule: **an encoded frame must be sent**. Flow-control drops happen _before_ encoding, by accumulating damage and encoding once later against the same `prev`. Dropping after encoding leaves the client holding pixels the encoder believes it already has, and the window is subtly wrong until the next keyframe.
- **Ack-driven flow control, two frames in flight.** An SSH channel buffers happily and will turn a slow link into seconds of latency. Three in flight is felt while dragging; one stalls on any real round-trip time.
- **One codec is wrong for this workload**, so `TierSelector` watches per-frame coverage and moves between lossless zstd rectangles, VP9 and WebP tiles with hysteresis (enter video at 0.35, leave at 0.15) — flipping tiers costs a keyframe, and a window sitting on a threshold would otherwise thrash. Opening a menu repaints everything once and must not turn a text editor into a video stream.
- **VP9, not H.264, and that is a licence decision.** x264 is GPL and cannot be linked into a BUSL binary we distribute; openh264's patent umbrella covers Cisco's own builds, not ours. libvpx is BSD-3 and royalty-free, VP9 decode is universal in Chromium (so always present in Electron) and `WebCodecs` covers the browsers. The no-WebCodecs fallback is WebP tiles, which the browser decodes natively — no shipped decoder at all.
