- **The launch environment is where "works on a bare cloud VM" is won.** Stock server images have no GPU, often no mesa, and frequently no `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` (pam_systemd creates it at login; an SSH session on a minimal image may never have had one). `launch_env` strips the host's X11 session, points every toolkit at our socket and forces software rendering — `GSK_RENDERER=cairo` is load-bearing, since GTK4 defaults to a GL renderer and dies outright without mesa. The fallback runtime dir is 0700 under `/tmp`, because Wayland refuses a socket in a group-writable directory.
- **A parentless toplevel is a tab; anything with a parent is not.** Without that rule, opening a menu spawns a workspace tab. The two parented kinds travel differently, and both halves shipped Aug 2026:
  - **Popups (`xdg_popup`) composite server-side.** `PopupRec`s in `compositor/state.rs` join the window's paint walk as extra roots at the positioner's offset (constrained by `get_unconstrained_geometry`, then clamped by `paint::place_popup`); input is hit-tested topmost-popup-first (`pointer_target`), a grab owns the keyboard (`keyboard_target`) and a press outside sends `popup_done` (`dismiss_popups_outside`). Three things had made popups no-ops, each fatal alone: no initial `xdg_surface.configure` (the client may not attach a buffer before one — the padlock panel waited forever), commits routed by subsurface parent only (a popup's root is itself, so its buffers were dropped), and input hard-focused on the toplevel. The initial configure is sent from `commit`, as the protocol orders it. Popups also need `send_frame_callbacks` in `take_frame` or they render once and freeze.
  - **Dialogs (parented toplevels) stay separate streams; the viewer overlays them.** `parent_changed` is the load-bearing hook: smithay raises `new_toplevel` on `get_toplevel`, _before_ the client sends `set_parent`, so a parent sampled at creation is almost always `None` — which is why dialogs used to open their own tabs. `AppWindowViewer` watches the session's window list and renders every window whose `parentWindowId` is its own as a recursive `dialog`-mode viewer: scrim overlay, centred, sized by the dialog's frames (attach at the host-reported size, no ResizeObserver echo), auto-focused, no per-dialog audio acquisition.
  - **A full recomposite now reports full-window damage** (`composite`'s tail): a popup closing or a subsurface moving damages nothing itself, and the old partial report left the vacated pixels stale on the client. Over-reporting is safe — the encoder diffs against what it last sent.
- **Desktop-entry rules that bite**: `Exec` field codes must be stripped (a bare `%U` disappears rather than becoming an empty argument, which otherwise makes apps open a file named ""), keys are localised most-specific-first, `[Desktop Action …]` groups must not bleed into the entry's own `Name`/`Exec`, and a hidden user override has to **claim its id** so the system copy does not reappear from a lower-precedence directory — that empty `NoDisplay=true` file is exactly how distributions hide an entry.
- **Icon lookup ranks theme, then size fit, then format.** Format after size, or a 48px PNG beats the scalable SVG when the caller asked for 256. Icons are capped at 6 KB and step down through smaller sizes, because workspace tabs persist to `localStorage` and thirty open tabs share that budget; XPM is dropped outright (no browser renders it), SVG is kept (an `<img>` renders it natively).
- **Paint parents before children, and blend.** A window is a surface _tree_, and Firefox is the case that proves it: its toplevel carries only the GTK shadow frame while the entire browser lives in a subsurface. `with_surface_tree_downward`'s post-order callback visits children first, so compositing there paints the mostly transparent parent over the content — an empty window from a client that drew everything correctly, which is exactly what the first captures produced. Paint on the way down (the traversal-action closure, where the subsurface offset is accumulated) and blend source-over with premultiplied alpha; a straight copy punches a hole wherever a surface is transparent.
- **`Output::enter` on map.** A surface that belongs to no output reads as "not visible" to some clients, which then stop painting.
- **Frame callbacks fire when a frame is _consumed_, not when it is committed**, which paces an application to the rate we can ship rather than to how fast it can render.
- **The client half is `@infrawrench/appstream-core`** (`plugin-architecture/packages/`), transport-free and DOM-free so Electron's main process, the web server and the browser all speak the same frames: envelope codec, control messages, packed input with the `KeyboardEvent.code` → evdev table, pixel-payload decode, and an `AppSession` that queues requests until the handshake lands and acks a frame only after the consumer has painted it (acking on arrival would let frames queue ahead of a slow viewer).
- **The two halves are pinned by golden fixtures, not by types.** `crates/iw-codec/tests/golden.rs` writes `appstream-core/fixtures/` — a deterministic four-frame sequence in the raw, zstd and JPEG tiers, plus the RGBA canvas the lossless ones reconstruct — and fails when the encoder's bytes drift from what is checked in; the TypeScript test decodes those exact bytes and asserts the same canvas. Regenerate deliberately with `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test -p iw-codec --test golden`, and expect the TS test to fail in the same commit if the format really moved. The fixture also pins the ~5× the lossless tier is buying, since a stream of incompressible noise would decode perfectly and quietly cost the bandwidth. There is deliberately **no canvas fixture for the JPEG tier** — its pixels depend on whichever decoder the client has, which is the same fact the encoder's lossy-tile tracking exists for — so what the fixture pins there is the framing and that each tile's own header describes its rectangle. Both sides assert the fixture still covers what it claims to (a delta op is present, a JPEG payload is present), because a fixture that quietly stopped exercising a tier would keep passing forever.
- **Three ways a rectangle reaches the client, and the rule that keeps them consistent.** `RectOp::Solid` is a fill; `RectOp::Pixels` is the pixels; `RectOp::Delta` is a per-byte wrapping difference from what the client already holds, zstd'd — interframe compression, and worth about 30% on the fixture sequence. A delta is used only when most of its bytes came out zero (`DELTA_ZERO_FRACTION`), because a rectangle that genuinely changed everywhere deltas to noise and compresses _worse_ than the pixels did. Two traps: the client canvas is a `Uint8ClampedArray`, which **clamps** what it is assigned, so the addition has to be masked to 8 bits before the store or a channel near 255 drifts and stays drifted; and a client that does not know the op would paint the differences as an image, so it is gated on a `delta` cap that defaults to **false** on the wire.
- **The lossy tier is JPEG, one image per damaged rectangle** (`Codec::JpegTiles`, `u32` length-prefixed, in table order). Chosen over anything else because the decoder is already in every browser — `createImageBitmap` — so the tier costs an encoder on the host and nothing at all on the client. `Tier::Image` is where a window in motion goes now: VP9 has no encoder, so before this a video simply stayed on the lossless tier and cost what it cost.
- **A lossy rectangle poisons its region for interframe purposes, and the encoder tracks that.** The client's copy of a JPEG rectangle is what _its_ decoder produced, which differs from ours by a unit or two per channel — invisible alone, permanent if a later delta is computed against it. So `Encoder` keeps a 64px tile grid marking which regions the client holds lossily, never deltas across one, and clears a tile only when a rectangle wholly covers it. Leaving the lossy mode forces a keyframe (`set_mode` returns whether one is needed), which is what makes text sharp again after a video stops.
- **Motion has to decay on quiet, not just rise on frames.** Coverage is only observed when a frame is encoded, so a paused video would sit on the lossy tier forever — showing a JPEG of a still picture the user is now trying to read. `Session::pump` therefore observes a zero for an attached window that produced nothing, and deliberately does _not_ for one that is out of in-flight slots: that window is the busiest there is, not the quietest.
- **HiDPI is one integer on the output, and everything else follows from it.** The viewer asks for its CSS box times its device pixel ratio; `configure` rounds that ratio **up** to a whole number (capped at `MAX_SCALE` = 3), sets it on the `wl_output`, and configures the toplevel at `physical / scale` _logical_ pixels — a toolkit renders at the scale of the output its surface entered, so it produces the buffer we wanted. Rounding up rather than to nearest means a 1.5× display gets a 2× buffer the browser downsamples: fractional scaling would save the difference in bandwidth but not add detail, and still needs `wp_fractional_scale_v1` (the server now implements `wp_viewporter` — see the viewporter bullet — but not the fractional protocol). Three details are load-bearing: `wl_compositor` v6 clients (GTK4, Qt6) take the scale from `send_surface_state` rather than from the output, a mapped surface has to `leave`/`enter` the output to hear about a change, and subsurface offsets and `wl_surface.damage` arrive in **logical** pixels while everything downstream is in buffer pixels — miss that and a HiDPI window composites its children at half their offsets and repaints a quarter of what it should. The viewer's canvas is `imageRendering: auto`, not `pixelated`, because at a fractional ratio it is downsampling.
- **The lossy tier is bandwidth-bound before it is CPU-bound, and the encoder now says so.** A full 2× window at quality 72 is well over a megabyte; nothing carries that per frame over SSH, so the frames queue and every one arrives late however fast the host produced it. `target_frame_bytes` (256 KB) is a closed loop on the encoded size — quality drops 6 when a frame overshoots and creeps back 2 when it lands under half, with a floor at 35 where text inside a moving window is still legible. Down fast, up slow, for the same reason every video call does it that way.
- **JPEG is the most expensive thing the encoder does, by an order of magnitude, so it is what got parallelised.** Measured on a 2400×1600 frame of pure noise (the worst case for every codec here): the interframe delta is 1.3ms, zstd is 2–5ms, and a single-threaded JPEG of the same frame was ~20ms. Large rectangles are cut into horizontal bands and encoded on `std::thread::scope` — no dependency, and the wire already carries one image per rectangle, so the split needed no format change. Bands are sized by **bytes, not by core count**, so a window produces the same frames on every host and the golden fixture stays reproducible; band heights round up to a multiple of 8 so none starts mid-block.
- **Hand-written SIMD bought less than expected, and the measurement is the point.** `simd.rs` carries SSE2/AVX2 and NEON kernels for the two per-pixel loops — the interframe difference with its zero count, and the uniform-colour test — dispatched at runtime on x86-64 and unconditionally on AArch64, where NEON is baseline. On an M-series core the delta kernel is **1.4×** the autovectorised scalar version and the uniform test **2.1×**: real, but nowhere near the order of magnitude the JPEG path was hiding. Every kernel has a scalar twin and a test asserting they agree at lengths either side of each vector width, because "wrong on the tail" is that file's entire failure mode; the tests reach past the dispatcher so CI exercises the paths the developer's machine does not have.
- **`jpeg-encoder`'s `simd` feature is x86-only**, AVX2 chosen at runtime, which is why the shipped baseline build still benefits from it. It also makes the encoder's exact bytes CPU-dependent, so the JPEG golden fixture pins the frame _shape_ — codec, keyframe flag, rectangle table — rather than the bytes. AArch64 hosts get no SIMD from that library at all; NEON colour conversion and FDCT would be an upstream contribution, and it is the largest single win left on ARM.
- **Everything on the hot path has to cost what _changed_, not what the window is.** Four places got this wrong at once, and every one of them quadrupled when HiDPI landed. `absorb` copied the whole `wl_shm` buffer per commit; `composite` allocated, zeroed and alpha-blended a fresh canvas per commit, with the canvas-bounds test _inside_ the per-pixel loop; the viewer handed `putImageData` the entire canvas per frame; and the BGRA→RGBA unpack moved one byte at a time. A character typed into a terminal cost the same as a full-screen video frame. Now: damage decides what `absorb` copies (which is what damage _means_ — the client promises the rest of the new buffer matches what the compositor holds, and double buffering does not break that), the canvas is kept between commits and only the damaged regions are re-composited, an opaque surface composites by row copy instead of per-pixel blending, the viewer uploads only the payload's bounding box, and the unpack goes a 32-bit word at a time when both sides are aligned. The word path is little-endian-only and falls back by feature test, because a payload's pixels can start at any offset in the frame they arrived in.
- **The clipboard was a protocol with nothing behind it.** Both halves existed as messages — `clipboardOffer`, `clipboardRequest`, a binary frame kind — and neither end implemented any of it: the host stored an offered blob in a field nothing read, `request_clipboard` was an empty `Ok(())`, and no UI on either platform ever sent or received one. The docs said it worked. Now: `offer_clipboard` publishes the text as the seat's selection with `set_data_device_selection`, so an application asking for the clipboard finds one; `send_selection` writes the bytes into the requesting client's pipe **on a thread**, because a compositor blocked on one application's read has stopped drawing for everybody; `new_selection` reports an application taking the clipboard as an offer, and `request_clipboard` opens a pipe, asks for it, and reads it off-thread, waking the loop when it lands. Contents are fetched on the _offer_ rather than on the paste, so a paste is instant and an unused selection costs nothing.
- **Pasting is synthesised, not forwarded.** The browser's paste shortcut is deliberately not intercepted — reading the clipboard ourselves needs a permission prompt, where letting the shortcut through produces a `paste` event carrying the text for free. The keystroke is then _not_ relayed: the application asks the compositor for the selection the moment it sees the key, so the text has to be published first, and a Mac user's `Cmd+V` would reach a Linux application as Meta+V and do nothing. So the viewer offers the text and then synthesises Ctrl+V. The other direction is best-effort by nature: `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is refused from a background tab, and the copy happens whenever the application decides to, not in response to anything the user did in the browser.
- **Audio is a PulseAudio server we implement, not one we find.** A headless VM has no sound server, so `iwappd` listens on its own socket (`crates/iwappd/src/pulse/`, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/iw-pulse-<session>/native`) and `launch_env` points `PULSE_SERVER` at it — the same call as bundling the compositor instead of requiring an X server. libpulse is the one audio client library everything links (including apps that think they are talking to PipeWire, via its pulse shim), so speaking its native protocol covers GTK, Qt, SDL, Firefox and Electron in one move; the protocol subset is hand-rolled over the existing deps (tagstructs are just tagged big-endian bytes) rather than linking libpulse, which a static musl build could not do anyway. SHM and memfd are refused in the handshake so every sample crosses the socket — a copy, in exchange for not implementing shared-memory block management. Record streams are refused: the viewer offers no microphone. Verified against the real client library, not just our own reading of it: `crates/iwappd/tests/pulse_live.rs` drives the server with `pactl` and `paplay` and skips where pulseaudio-utils is not installed (CI has only libxkbcommon-dev, so it runs on laptops).
- **The pulse module is sans-io like `Session`, and that split is what makes it testable.** `pulse/server.rs` is bytes-and-clock-in, reply-bytes-and-PCM-out — connection state machine, per-stream rings with PA's seek/cork/prebuf/drain semantics, format conversion (u8/s16/s24/s32/f32, both endians), linear resampling and mixing all run in unit tests on any OS. `pulse/runtime.rs` (cfg unix) owns the threads: an accept loop, a blocking reader per client, and a mixer ticking every 10 ms that emits 48 kHz stereo s16 chunks, zstd level 1 with a raw fallback when compression does not pay. The mixer paces itself by elapsed time, not tick count, and drops backlog past 100 ms — a suspended laptop must not burst its missing seconds at the client.
- **Audio frames ride the same FIFO as pixels, and the client absorbs that.** `FrameKind::Audio` (0x84, `AudioChunk` in iw-proto, pinned by `audio-frames.bin`/`audio-pcm.s16` in the golden fixtures) shares the ordered SSH stream with 256 KiB pixel frames, so head-of-line jitter is structural. The viewer's `SessionAudio` (`ui/src/apps/session-audio.ts`) schedules chunks 150 ms behind the Web Audio clock and grows the lead on underrun; a `seq` gap or the chunk's reset flag restarts the clock instead of stretching. `GetPlaybackLatency` reports a stand-in 150 ms for the same reason — the honest figure is the link plus the jitter buffer, which the host cannot know, and a video player shifting its picture by roughly the truth beats not shifting it at all.
- **The audio capability gates in both directions, and mute stops the stream at the source.** `ClientCaps.audio` wire-defaults to false because an unknown frame kind is a thrown `ProtocolError` on the client — sending audio to an old client would kill its whole session, which is the same reason `delta` defaults false. The client only probes true where `AudioContext` exists. Muting sends `setAudio { enabled: false }` so the PCM stops crossing the link rather than being played into a zero gain, and the last viewer tab to unmount does the same — chunks nobody would play are bandwidth spent on nothing. One player per session, acquired ref-counted by the shared `AppWindowViewer`, because the host mixes everything into one stream and two players would double it.
- **A surface tree may mix buffer scales, and copying those pixels one for one is wrong.** Firefox does it: the toplevel takes the output's 2 while the content subsurface stays at 1, and a straight copy then draws the whole page at half size in the corner of its own window with the rest of the canvas unpainted. `paint::blit` samples rather than copies whenever the source's scale differs from the canvas's, and damage from such a surface is rescaled outwards — covering a pixel that did not change costs a few bytes, missing one that did leaves it stale until something else repaints it. The equal-scale path is still a row copy, which is every window that is not mixed.
- **`wp_viewporter` is not optional, because Firefox's software renderer does HiDPI through it and nothing else.** On a 2× output Firefox renders its content at device resolution into a buffer committed at `buffer_scale` **1** and declares the logical size with `wp_viewport.set_destination` — the buffer/scale arithmetic alone reads that as a window twice its logical size, drawn magnified by the scale and cropped to its own canvas, which shipped as "everything in the streamed app is twice as big and cut off" on every retina viewer while `foot` and GTK4 apps were pixel-perfect. Every desktop compositor advertises viewporter, so clients' no-viewporter fallbacks are effectively untested territory; this was proven by black-box bisection against headless sway (`WLR_BACKENDS=headless`, `output ... scale 2`, identical `MOZ_LOG=Widget*` scale bookkeeping, perfect rendering) and by `IWAPPD_DEBUG=1` showing the content subsurface committing 1600×1200 at scale 1 for an 800×600-logical window. The compositing pass honours the mapping end to end: `SurfacePixels` carries the committed src/dst, `blit` samples source-to-destination (`dest_logical` × canvas scale wins over the scale ratio), the layout records the box a surface is _shown_ in so a viewport change reads as a layout change, and damage crosses via `rescale_to` (box-to-box, outwards) rather than the integer-pair rescale. Relatedly, the output's **mode is physical pixels**: held at a fixed 1920×1080 while the scale rose, the logical desktop shrank below the viewer's tab and toolkits clamped their windows to it (Firefox visibly resized itself at scale 3), so the desktop is now tracked in logical pixels, grows to fit the largest configured window, and the mode is advertised as desktop × scale.
- **The compositing arithmetic lives in `paint.rs`, outside the compositor module, so it tests on a laptop.** Anything under `compositor/` needs `libxkbcommon` to _link_, so its tests only run where that exists — `cargo clippy` passes without it and hides this. Moving the rectangle-and-byte half out found a wrong assertion the moment it could execute. Same reasoning as `keymap.rs`: keep the parts that are pure arithmetic away from the parts that are Wayland.
- **Applications are asked to exit before they are killed.** `Child::kill` is SIGKILL, and Firefox counts that as a crash — so a clean shutdown of ours greeted the _next_ session with "we're having trouble getting your pages back". `terminate_all` sends SIGTERM to the process _group_ (each child leads its own, which is why the group is addressable), polls for up to 1.5s, and only then kills. Signalling the group rather than the process also matters on its own: a browser is many processes, and signalling the one we spawned leaves the rest running on the customer's machine.
- **A subsurface that moves damages nothing.** Damage says what changed _within_ a surface, so a menu sliding across a window leaves no damage covering the pixels it vacated — patch-only compositing would smear it. `WindowRec.layout` records where every surface sat, and any change to it forces a full recomposite. That is also what covers a surface losing its buffer, since its size in the layout goes to zero.
- **The host's keymap is `us` and cannot be anything else, so the _character_ travels rather than the position.** The browser will not say what layout is in use and there is no protocol for asking, so forwarding physical keycodes — which the original design did, reasoning that "the host resolves the character through its own keymap" — is correct only for a user already on US QWERTY. Everyone else gets the wrong table: a UK user types `"` and receives `@`, an AZERTY user types `a` and receives `q`. `KeyTranslator` (`appstream-core/src/keys.ts`) maps `KeyboardEvent.key` to whichever US key produces that character, synthesising Shift where the two layouts disagree and putting it back immediately — the character is decided when the key goes down, and the user may release Shift while still holding the key. Caps Lock has to be _un_-applied for letters, since `key` already reflects it and the host's own Caps Lock applies again. A press may therefore go out as a different keycode than the one pressed, which is why the translator is stateful: the release has to match.
- **What no US key can produce goes as a keysym, and the compositor binds it a keycode.** `£`, `é`, anything an input method composed. `SpareKeys` hands out evdev codes from 200 and `keymap::inject` appends them to the keymap xkbcommon already compiled — appending to the _dumped_ text rather than re-resolving the xkb rules, because the dump is self-contained and a host with no `xkeyboard-config` therefore cannot lose a working keyboard to a failed recompile. Bindings accumulate rather than swapping per keystroke: a language's accents are a handful of keys and after the first few nothing changes, which matters because every client recompiles the keymap on each swap. The spare keys are `ONE_LEVEL` so a held Shift cannot reach a level that is not there. All of it is string manipulation in a platform-neutral module, so it tests on a machine with no Wayland; only the compile is Linux's, and a compile that fails keeps the old keymap and drops the character.
- **A GTK4 application with no session bus never maps a window.** It does not fail — it waits, so the launcher shows nothing, the host logs nothing, and the only symptom is an application that does not appear. `iwappd` resolves the bus once at startup (`resolve_session_bus`): an inherited `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`, else the socket systemd leaves at `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bus` — named explicitly, because the toolkits that do not implement libdbus's convention would not find it — else `dbus-run-session --` prefixed onto every launch, which is a _command_ change rather than an environment one because the address does not exist until that process starts. A host with none of the three gets a line in the log saying so. The decision table is unit-tested off Linux by taking what it found rather than looking itself.
- **`iwappd` is the accessibility registry, not just a compositor.** Toolkits publish their widget trees over AT-SPI to whoever owns `org.a11y.atspi.Registry` on the session bus; on a desktop that is `at-spi2-registryd`, and a headless VM has nobody — so `iwappd` claims the name itself, answers each application's `Embed`, and walks a window's tree with ordinary D-Bus method calls (`crates/iwappd/src/atspi/`). This is why the `a11yTree` capability is gated on `SessionBus::Address`: a per-application `dbus-run-session` bus puts each tree where nobody else can dial it, and a host with no bus has none at all. The D-Bus client is **hand-rolled** over the existing deps (the same call as the PulseAudio server — a full D-Bus crate brings an async runtime, and none of it clears the "runs on someone else's machine" bar), decoding only the wire subset AT-SPI uses, little-endian only, big-endian messages skipped by length rather than misread. `launch_env::apply_a11y` turns the bridges on (`AT_SPI_BUS_ADDRESS`, `GTK_MODULES=…:gail:atk-bridge`, `QT_LINUX_ACCESSIBILITY_ALWAYS_ON`) and strips an inherited `NO_AT_BRIDGE`. The `AtspiRole`/`AtspiStateType` tables in `atspi/names.rs` are transcribed from `atspi-constants.h` by wire number — verified against the header, not memory — and an unknown value degrades to `role-<n>` rather than dropping the node. The whole walk runs on its own thread with its own bus connection (a tree is thousands of round trips and the serve loop has frames to encode), answers `Embed` even mid-walk, and is covered end-to-end by `atspi::tests` against a real `dbus-daemon` (skips where none is installed, like the pulse live test).
- **The headless driver is the other consumer of `appstream-core`, beside the browser viewer.** `HeadlessAppClient` (`appstream-host/src/headless.ts`) keeps the same per-window RGBA canvas the `AppWindowViewer` canvas does — same `applyPayload` — but with **lossless-only caps** (`jpeg/webp/vp9` all false), so every frame reconstructs exactly and a screenshot is never a compression artefact; `screenshot()` waits for the window to go quiet, then encodes the canvas as PNG (`appstream-host/src/png.ts`, `node:zlib`, no image dep, mirroring the Rust `png.rs`). Input is synthesised through the same `KeyTranslator` the viewer uses, so typing survives the US-keymap translation. The web server drives it through `services/apps-headless.ts` (sessions cached per `org:resource`, torn down on a 5-minute idle, host resolved by the same `resolveSshConfig`/`sshEndpoint` path as `ssh_exec`), exposed as the MCP/chat tools in `tools/linux-apps.ts` — `screenshot_app_window`, `read_app_accessibility_tree`, `click_app_window`, `type_in_app_window`, etc., all on `resources:execute`. Screenshot pixels, click coordinates and a11y bounds are one space. **`appstream-host/src/index.ts` is now a re-export barrel over `server.ts` (staging/exec) and `headless.ts`** — the driver imports the server, so the split is what avoids an import cycle through the index.
- **A tool result can carry an image, on a side channel.** `ToolResult.images?` (`web/src/tools/types.ts`, via `okImage`) is base64 blocks the MCP server forwards to the client as native image content so a model can see a screenshot; the chat surface ignores them, because its persisted content contract (`ChatContentBlock` in `client-core`) is text-only and shared with mobile — the text `content` is a caption there. Don't widen the chat contract to carry images without touching every provider and mobile.
- **On this server, an unhandled event ends everybody's session.** The web process holds long-lived state for many people — SSH shells, SQL connections, application streams — and Node's default for an unhandled rejection or an unlistened-to `error` event is to end the process, which reaches the user as a gateway error on every one of those sessions at once. Three places in the apps path could do it: `ws.on("error")` was registered _after_ the seconds of connecting, staging and starting rather than before (a reload in that window is an ECONNRESET nobody was listening for — the SSH terminal proxy comments on registering its teardown before dialling, and this did not); the exec channel and its stderr had no `error` listener at all, so a dropped connection took the process rather than the session; and `server.on("upgrade", async …)` turned any rejection inside it — a database blip while resolving a token — into an unhandled rejection. All three are fixed at the source, and `installProcessGuards` in `server.ts` logs and survives the next one rather than exiting. Writing to a dead channel is swallowed for the same reason: the relay writes from a WebSocket message handler, where a throw is the process and not the caller.
- **A wheel event needs discrete steps, or toolkits ignore it.** `wl_pointer` v8 clients read `axis_value120` and v5–7 read `axis_discrete`; Smithay emits either only if the frame carries `.v120()`. A wheel frame with just a continuous value is something a toolkit is free to ignore, and enough of them do that scrolling looked broken. The client normalises every wheel to Wayland's "ten units per notch", so a notch is twelve times that in v120 units — `v120_from_axis` in `iw-proto`, where it is testable off Linux. A wheel also has to carry the pointer's **position**: a compositor delivers an axis event to whatever the pointer is over, so a scroll with no motion behind it goes nowhere until the mouse has moved.
- **Key repeat is the browser's alone; the application's is disabled.** Wayland repeat is a hold-timer in the client (`wl_keyboard.repeat_info`), and over this link "held" includes the network: with `add_keyboard(.., 200, 25)` a tapped key whose release frame arrived late read as a 200ms hold, and Firefox typed characters nobody pressed — sporadic doubled letters that got worse with latency. The compositor now advertises rate 0 (which the protocol defines as repeat disabled), and `KeyTranslator.press` forwards the browser's real auto-repeat instead, as a release-and-press re-tap of whatever the key went out as — re-entered rather than replayed, because Shift may have changed mid-hold. So repeat is driven by keystrokes that actually happened, at the user's own OS repeat settings, and latency cannot invent any. Separately, a key held when the canvas loses focus never gets its `keyup`: it goes to whatever has focus now, and the application is left believing the key is down — a stuck modifier at best. The viewer tracks what is down and releases it on blur and on unmount. Both are pinned by `ui/src/__tests__/app-window-input.test.tsx`, which stubs `ImageData` and `getContext` because jsdom has no canvas.
- **Client input wakes the event loop.** `dispatch` blocks for a turn (8ms), and stdin is read on another thread, so without a `calloop` ping a keystroke could sit in the channel for a whole turn before anything looked at it — on every key and every mouse move. The reader pings after each chunk.
- **The serve loop reports what it spent, to stderr, every five seconds of activity** (`[stats] … compositing Xms/s, encoding Yms/s (slowest frame Zms), N KiB/s`). Both apps already forward the server's stderr into their logs. Splitting compositing from encoding is the point: "the host is slow at drawing" and "the host is slow at compressing" look identical from the outside and want opposite fixes. A quiet session prints nothing.
- **Node's `zstdDecompressSync` stands in for the wasm decoder in tests** (Node 22.15+). The browser still needs the wasm module; the fixture test only needs _a_ zstd.
- **`@infrawrench/appstream-host` is what puts the binary on a host and runs it**, shared because both apps do exactly the same thing over connections they each opened their own way (desktop through `electron/ssh-shell.ts`, web through `services/ssh-proxy.ts`). It takes a structurally-typed executor rather than an ssh2 `Client`, so it declares no dependency on ssh2 and a test can drive it with a fake.
- **The binary is never installed on the customer's machine.** It is written to the first RAM-backed directory that is writable _and_ exec-capable (`/dev/shm`, `/run/user/<uid>`, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, then `/tmp`), opened, unlinked, and executed through `/proc/self/fd/3` — so from the moment it starts there is no file, and nothing survives the session, a dropped connection or a crash. Verified on a real host: the staged file is gone before the process prints its version. The exec-capability probe matters because a hardened host mounts `/tmp` and `/dev/shm` `noexec`, and finding that out by failing to exec is a far worse error. A watchdog removes the staged file after a minute regardless, in case the client dies between staging and starting. The cost is ~950 KB of upload per session, which is the right trade for not leaving an executable behind.
- **Starting the server takes two channels, listing apps takes one.** The upload arrives on stdin, and the server's stdin then has to carry protocol frames — so staging and running cannot share a channel. `--list-apps` needs no stdin of its own, so its upload, run and delete fit in a single exec.
- **`libxkbcommon-dev` is a build dependency on Linux**, including for `cargo test`, because linking the test binaries links the compositor. `cargo clippy` passes without it — checking does not link — so a CI job that lints but cannot test looks green until the test step runs.
- **The static binary must be built inside Alpine.** The compositor links `libxkbcommon`; a static musl build needs a musl build of that library, and Debian and the `cross` images carry only the glibc one (`cannot find -lxkbcommon`). Alpine packages `libxkbcommon-static`, and both architectures build natively on their own runner — `docker run` rather than a job-level `container:`, because `actions/checkout` needs a glibc node. ~2.5 MB, `static-pie linked`.
- **Two findings about testing against real applications.** A GTK4 app needs `dbus-run-session` or it never maps a window. And Firefox counts every kill as a crash, so a capture harness that terminates it repeatedly lands it in "Open Firefox in Troubleshoot Mode?" — which then _is_ the window you photograph. Test profiles need `toolkit.startup.max_resumed_crashes = -1`.
- **Both apps reach it the same way, through two packages.** `@infrawrench/appstream-core` is the wire (frames, control messages, input packing, pixel decode, an `AppSession` that queues until the handshake and acks after the consumer paints); `@infrawrench/appstream-host` is the host side. The desktop opens the connection with `connectSshChain` — extracted from `ssh-shell.ts` so jump hosts, agent forwarding and the TOFU check behave exactly as a terminal does — and relays frames over IPC; the web server holds the connection itself behind `/api/apps`, gated on the same ws-token and `resources:execute` scope, and refuses internal address space through `resolveSafeHost` before dialling.
- **A cloud key on the desktop means the cloud is the agent, not the transport.** A cloud-held org key's private half never leaves the server, and the desktop's answer is deliberately _not_ to hairpin the app stream through `/api/apps` — pixels stay on the direct desktop→host connection, and only publickey-auth signatures cross the cloud. The pieces: `POST /ssh-keys/:id/sign` (`web/src/api/routes/ssh-keys.ts`, gated on `resources:execute` because a signature is shell-grade authority — same reasoning as `/api/ws` — audited as `ssh.agent.sign[_failed]`, refuses imported keys, 16 KiB cap on the challenge); `signSshData`/`signatureAlgorithmFor` and `RemoteKeyAgent` in `@infrawrench/ssh-tunnel-core` (the agent-protocol framing now lives in `agent-wire.ts`, shared with `InProcessAgent`; `makeAgentStream` chains replies so an async signer cannot reorder them; the server returns the _raw_ `ParsedKey.sign` bytes because ssh2's `authPK` runs agent signatures through `convertSignature`, and the agent converts DER ECDSA itself only on the forwarded-agent path); and in the desktop main process `CLOUD_KEY_SENTINEL` + `SshShellConfig.cloudKey`, resolved inside `connectSshChain` to a `buildCloudKeyAgent` (`electron/cloud-key-agent.ts`, `cloudFetch`-backed) — so the apps pane, `apps_list`, and anything else on that chain gets cloud keys for free, and a terminal could adopt the same sentinel later. Desktop cloud-key _terminals_ still dispatch through the WS proxy on purpose: session recording and shared consoles live server-side. The renderer sends only `{orgId, sshKeyId}`; the main process fetches the public half itself.
- **A session belongs to a resource, not to an address.** The registry in each app's `lib/apps-session.ts` is keyed `accountId::resourceId` and reference-counted, so the launcher and every window tab share one connection and one compositor. A window tab has no key and no address of its own — it _joins_ — which is why a reload leaves it saying so rather than silently blank, and why closing the Apps tab ends its windows.
- **A launch has no success signal of its own, so the failures must be shown.** Launching produces a window, which becomes a tab somewhere else entirely; when it fails it produces nothing at all, and the launcher would otherwise sit there looking exactly as it did before the click. The host reports a failure two ways — `launchResult { ok: false }` for an entry it refused outright, and an `error` frame carrying `unknownApp` or `launchFailed` for a child that was spawned and died (the message is the child's own stderr, which on a bare host is the missing library, named) — and `AppSession` normalises both into `LaunchResult` and fans them out to `addLaunchResultListener`. Those two codes are deliberately **not** routed to `onError`: both apps map that to a session-wide error state, and one broken desktop entry would paint the launcher red for good while every other application still starts fine. A new error code has to be classified the same way, or it lands in the wrong half of that split.
- **A host is checked before a session is opened, and the check cannot use the thing it is checking.** A bare cloud image is missing four things that each fail without saying so: no `gunzip` and the upload cannot be unpacked; no `xkeyboard-config` and xkbcommon cannot compile a keymap, so the keyboard silently does nothing; no session bus and a GTK4 app waits forever without mapping a window; no fonts and Qt exits while GTK draws boxes. All four reach the user as "I clicked it and nothing happened". So `appstream-host/src/preflight.ts` probes first — and because staging `iwappd` needs the `gunzip` it is checking for, the probe is **plain POSIX `sh` in one exec**, not an `iwappd` mode. It prints `key=value` lines rather than JSON for the same reason `listApps` parses only the last line: a login banner on stdout would break `JSON.parse`, where here it is just a line with no `=` in it. The staging check reuses `pickStagingDirScript()` verbatim, so the probe cannot pass a directory the upload then fails on, and `noexec` is reported as the one condition no package fixes.
- **The install takes requirement ids, never commands, and is verified by re-probing.** `planInstall` maps missing ids to that host's package manager (`apt-get`/`dnf`/`yum`/`apk`/`pacman`/`zypper`, first match on PATH) and returns the exact command lines, which both UIs show _before_ the button — this installs packages as root on someone else's machine. Neither the renderer nor the browser can supply a command: the desktop's `apps_install` handler and web's `POST /apps/setup` each re-probe and rebuild the plan server-side, so there is no request shape that turns either into a remote root shell. Privilege is `root` or `sudo -n` only (never a plain `sudo` that could hang on a password nobody can type down an exec channel); a `sudo-password` or no-sudo host still gets the commands, with `canInstall: false`, because "run these yourself" beats "unsupported". The installer tries the batch then falls back to one package at a time, so a name a distribution spells differently costs that package rather than all of them — and the verdict comes from a **second probe**, since a package manager exits zero having fixed nothing and non-zero because one name out of five was wrong. Package names were checked against the distributions' own indexes, not from memory: `dbus-run-session` left `dbus` for `dbus-daemon` in Debian bookworm and lives in `dbus-daemon` on Fedora, which is why apt installs `dbus` (it depends on both, on every release) while dnf installs `dbus-daemon`.
- **The contract types live in `appstream-core`, not `appstream-host`.** `HostPreflight`, `InstallPlan`, `RequirementId` and friends are in `appstream-core/src/requirements.ts` even though nothing there crosses the `iw-proto` wire, because `@infrawrench/ui` renders them and cannot depend on `appstream-host`: that package is Node-typed (Buffers, ssh2 channels) and `ui` has no `@types/node` at all, so even a type-only import would fail to resolve `Buffer` in its declaration file. `appstream-host` imports and re-exports them. The English `title`/`summary` on each requirement is for the CLI; the UI has its own `switch` over literal ids returning `<T>`, because gt's extractor hard-errors on a non-literal argument and a string that arrived from a package is not one.
- **`useHostSetup` keys on a host string, not on the transport object.** The hook lives in `ui/src/apps/` because only its two calls differ per platform; everything around them is shared. Its check effect depends on a `hostKey` the caller spells out (`key|user@host`) and reads the transport from a ref, because both call sites build their transport inline from a config the router rebuilds every render — keying the effect on that object re-probes the host on every paint, which is a loop that spends the customer's SSH connections. `blocked` is deliberately **false while the check is in flight**: gating the session on an unanswered check would add a round trip to every launcher open for a prompt almost nobody sees. It is also false when the check _failed_, because a broken SSH connection is not a host missing everything, and a misleading checklist is worse than the real error the session will produce.
- **The viewer decompresses zstd in JS** (`fzstd`, ~10 KB, MIT) rather than shipping a wasm module. The format is standard, the golden fixtures prove cross-implementation agreement, and a wasm build remains an optimisation rather than a prerequisite.
- **Tabs, and what the window tab does at rest.** The launcher is a resource view (`view: "apps"`) beside SSH and SFTP; each window is a `linux-app` tab keyed by session and window id, routed to its resource's URL with the window in the query because a window URL means nothing without a live session. `validate-tabs` and the desktop's `validateWorkspaceTab` both drop `linux-app` tabs on restore for the same reason.
- **Outside every JS toolchain**, like the Terraform provider: not in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` or `turbo.json`, tested by its own `.github/workflows/linux-appserver.yml` (`cargo fmt --check`, `clippy -D warnings`, `cargo test`, plus static musl builds for x86_64 and aarch64 that assert the binary really is static). It **is** in `cliff.toml`'s `include_paths`, because the desktop app ships this binary. Runtime dependencies are `serde`, `thiserror`, `zstd` and `jpeg-encoder`, and the bar for a fifth is high — everything here runs on someone else's machine.
- **The two apps get the binaries by different routes, and that asymmetry is forced.** Both need the same thing — one gzipped static binary per architecture, ready to push over SSH — behind the same pair of functions, `getx86_64GzBinary()` and `getArm64GzBinary()`. The desktop ships `iwappd.tar.xz` as an `extraResources` entry and decompresses it on first use (`electron/iwappd-archive.ts`), because a laptop may have no route to our storage; `scripts/ensure-iwappd.mjs` puts the archive there at build time by hashing `linux-appserver/`, downloading that hash from R2 when CI has built it, and compiling in Docker when it has not. The web server _cannot_ do any of that: its image is built from `turbo prune @infrawrench/web --docker`, and `linux-appserver/` is outside the workspace so the pruned tree does not contain it — there is nothing to hash and nothing to pack. So `web/src/services/iwappd-binaries.ts` fetches at runtime instead, reading the `latest` pointer written by the `rust-latest` job to find the current hash and caching the gzipped result in process memory for 10 minutes. The pointer is what makes the TTL cheap: an unchanged build costs one small request rather than re-downloading and re-compressing megabytes, and a refresh that fails serves the stale entry rather than failing an enrolment. That pointer lives at the key `iwappd-builds/latest/iwappd.tar.xz` despite holding a hash rather than an archive, because the downloader Worker maps `/<key>` to `iwappd-builds/<key>/iwappd.tar.xz` and that is the only key `GET /latest` reaches.
- **Decompressing xz in Node means WebAssembly, not a native addon.** Both apps use `xz-decompress`. The obvious `xz` package cannot be installed: its build hardcodes the interpreter name `python`, which no longer exists on macOS or modern Linux, and its upstream repository has been deleted, so there is no fixing it upstream. Even built, a native addon would need a compiler on every dev machine and every packaging architecture to save maybe a megabyte on an artefact we control both ends of. One wrinkle survives the choice: `xz-decompress` is CJS whose named exports Node's `cjs-module-lexer` cannot see, so it must be imported as a default and destructured — a named import works in the bundled output and throws under `tsx watch`.

## Cross-replica session relay (`services/replica-relay.ts`)

Some sessions live in one web pod's memory and cannot be moved. The web Deployment runs `replicas: 2` behind round-robin routing, so roughly half of the calls about such a session arrive at a pod that does not hold it — and the pod they land on has no way to know it should not just start its own.

- **The failure this fixes was intermittent and misattributed.** A Linux application session is an SSH channel to `iwappd`, and `serve.rs` breaks its loop on `!stdin_open` — the compositor exits with the channel that opened it, so it can never be handed to another pod. When a second pod started its own compositor for the same session id it lost the Wayland socket bind (`Requested socket name is already in use`), exited, and the client reported only `the app server closed before greeting`. About one MCP app call in two, with no pattern a user could see.
- **The lease is the whole concurrency argument.** `replica_session_owners` holds one row per session (`${kind}:${key}` → `owner_address`), claimed with a single `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE … setWhere`. Two pods racing a new session both run one statement, Postgres serialises them, one insert wins and the loser reads the winner's address. `setWhere` is what stops a _live_ session being stolen: an existing lease is only overwritten when it is already ours or its holder has stopped heartbeating.
- **Heartbeats, not cleanup, are what make it correct.** The case that matters is the one where no cleanup runs — a pod OOM-killed, evicted mid-rollout, or partitioned. A lease older than `LEASE_TTL_MS` (60s) is claimable by anyone, so a dead pod strands a session for a minute rather than until someone notices. Teardown _also_ releases, but only as an optimisation.
- **Operations are written once and reached two ways.** `runLocally` in `apps-headless.ts` is the only implementation; the owning pod calls it directly and every other pod forwards to `POST /api/internal/relay`, which calls the same function. A new operation is a case in that switch plus a method on `AppsSession` — there is no second code path to keep in step. Every `AppSession` method is async even where the local one is synchronous, because on a non-owning pod they are network calls.
- **An unreachable owner is not an error.** A pod that vanished between the claim and the call (a rollout) surfaces as `RelayUnreachableError`, distinct from `RelayRemoteError` (the owner is fine, the operation failed). The first drops the lease and retries, so a pod dying costs a caller latency instead of a failed request.
- **It disables itself when it is not needed.** Without `POD_IP` (downward API) and `INTERNAL_RELAY_SECRET` every claim answers "self" — the exact single-process behaviour of a dev server, a test, and the desktop app. `POD_IP` set _without_ the secret warns and stays disabled rather than forwarding onto an endpoint that cannot authenticate its callers.
- **What authenticates the endpoint, stated honestly.** The shared secret, and nothing else. The forwarding pod already checked `resources:execute`; the secret is what makes "this came from one of our pods" a fact. Two things keep that from being the only control: the organization is part of the session key and is re-applied to the resource lookup on the receiving side, so a forwarded call cannot cross orgs however it is shaped; and `isForwardableAddress` restricts dialling to private IPv4, so a table row naming a public host (or `169.254.169.254`) cannot turn a replica into an open forwarder.
- **This is the mechanism `web-ws-ingress.yaml` was waiting for.** That file's `upstream-hash-by: "$arg_sid"` solves the browser half of the same problem for shared consoles and says outright that the durable fix is "a cross-replica relay — the same follow-up the bastion registry is waiting on". Consistent hashing cannot help the agent path at all: an MCP client posts to `/api/mcp` with the resource in the JSON body, which nginx cannot see. Shared consoles and the bastion registry are the other two intended consumers and have **not** been migrated yet; the `kind` column is there so they can be.
- **Still unmigrated: the browser viewer.** `apps-proxy.ts` calls `startAppServer` per WebSocket with the same `${org}-${resource}` session id, so two tabs on one resource collide even on a single replica. That needs a decision the relay does not make for it — whether a second viewer _attaches_ to the running session or gets its own — and until then it is the same bind failure with a clearer message.

## Accessibility conventions

Established during the July 2026 a11y sweep (react-doctor Accessibility findings: 78 → 0). Keep new code within these patterns:

- **Modals** — `ui/src/components/Modal.tsx` is a native `<dialog>` (free focus trap/restore, Escape via `cancel`, body scroll-lock). Always pass `ariaLabel` (the dialog's accessible name, usually the visible heading text). Backdrop click-away lives in an effect listener, not a JSX handler — keep it that way (jsx_a11y flags mouse handlers on `<dialog>`). SpotlightSearch uses the same native-dialog pattern with `backdrop:` Tailwind variants.
- **Form fields** — visible `<label>` + `htmlFor`/`id` wired via `useId()` (never hardcoded ids; components can mount twice). Composite pickers (CostFilterRows, KeyValueListEditor…) get a `<span>` caption + `role="group"`/`aria-labelledby`, with each inner control `aria-label`ed. Placeholder text is never the only name. Monaco editors are named via `options.ariaLabel`.
- **Hover-revealed controls** — every `opacity-0 group-hover:opacity-100` must also carry `group-focus-within:opacity-100` (+ `focus-visible:opacity-100` on the focusable element itself).
- **Draggable pills** — dnd-kit ref/listeners/attributes go on an inner native `<button>`; the styled wrapper stays non-interactive so pin/open/action buttons are siblings, not nested interactives (reference: `desktop/src/routes/_account-detail/-ResourcePill.tsx`).
- **Menus** — context menus and dropdowns use `role="menu"`/`menuitem`, `aria-expanded`/`aria-haspopup` on triggers, Escape-to-close with focus restore, ArrowUp/Down roving focus, and Shift+F10/ContextMenu-key as the keyboard right-click (reference: `ui/src/components/OrgSwitcher.tsx`, `desktop/src/components/SidebarAccounts.tsx`).
- **Async status** — loading/error/result-count changes go through `role="status"`/`role="alert"` (sr-only where there's no visible text); terminals mirror connection state into an sr-only status div; charts get `role="img"` + a summary `aria-label` (or `aria-hidden` when purely duplicative).
- **Clickable table rows** — the action goes on a real `<button>` in the first cell (the resource/zone/record name), never on the `<tr>`. A row can be given `tabIndex` and an Enter/Space handler, but there is no row role a screen reader announces as activatable, so it lands as a focus stop with no name and no affordance. The button also removes the whole-row click target, and with it the `stopPropagation` every sibling action (Delete, Dismiss, Restore, File issue) needed to escape it — the row keeps only `hover:bg-*`. Where column one is a badge rather than a name, give the button an `aria-label` (`Open <name>` / `Edit <name>`; see `ChildResourceTable`). References: `ui/src/{dns/DnsSection,expiry/ExpirySection,posture/PostureSection,savings/SavingsSection}.tsx`.
- **`aria-activedescendant` listboxes** (`MultiSelect`, `SpotlightSearch`) — focus stays on the `role="combobox"` input, which owns the entire keyboard path (Arrow/Home/End move the active index, Enter activates, Escape closes). Options carry `role="option"` + `tabIndex={-1}` + `onClick`, and that click is the **mouse half** of the pattern, not the only way in: an `onKeyDown` on an option would never fire, because the option never holds focus. Static linters flag it anyway (`click-events-have-key-events`) — leave the comment that says why. Only `option`/`group` may be children of the listbox: loading/empty/error/no-match copy goes in a sibling `role="status"`, and grouped results get a `role="group"` + `aria-labelledby` per header, or the headers are announced as selectable values.
- **Focusable SVG children** — Firefox and Safari do not paint CSS `outline` on SVG elements, so `theme.css`'s global `:focus-visible` rule is invisible on an SVG `<g role="button" tabIndex={0}>`. Draw the ring in SVG instead: `focus:outline-none` + a `group/…`-scoped `<rect>` revealed by `group-focus-visible/…:opacity-100` (reference: `ui/src/components/graph/DependencyGraphView.tsx`). Do **not** make an SVG backdrop focusable to satisfy a linter — the graph's transparent `<rect>` is `aria-hidden` and mouse-only on purpose, the same legitimate pattern as the modal backdrops, with Escape and a visible **Clear** button as the keyboard equivalent.
- **Skip link** — both shells (`{web,desktop}/src/routes/__root.tsx`) render `sr-only focus:not-sr-only` "Skip to content" as the first tab stop, targeting `<main id="main-content">`. Without it a keyboard user walks the tab strip and the whole sidebar again after every navigation. It is per-shell markup, so it has to be added to both.
- **Theme** — `theme.css` foreground tokens clear WCAG AA (4.5:1) against **all four** surfaces (surface, raised, overlay, sunken) in **both** schemes. `ui/src/__tests__/theme-contrast.test.ts` parses the stylesheet and enforces that, so a value that drifts fails the suite rather than shipping. Global `:focus-visible` outline and a `prefers-reduced-motion` kill-switch live at the bottom of `theme.css`.
- **Colour is a token, never a Tailwind palette class.** `text-red-400`, `text-amber-500`, `text-green-400` and friends are one fixed colour in both schemes, so they can only be legible in one of them: light mode is the default for anyone whose OS is not in dark mode, and against `--color-surface` (#ffffff) `text-red-400` measured 2.77:1 — the app's error text was its least readable text. The August 2026 sweep replaced all 841 such utilities with semantic tokens. Reach for:
  - `text-danger` / `text-warning` / `text-success` / `text-info` — status text, each with a `-strong` variant for the higher-emphasis step (hover, or a label on a tinted chip). `-strong` is _darker_ in light mode and _lighter_ in dark, so "stronger" always means "more contrast"; `text-danger hover:text-danger-strong` is the shape a `text-red-400 hover:text-red-500 dark:text-red-300` triple collapses to.
  - `text-severe` — the severity rung between warning and danger (posture `high`, expiry `critical`, `ALPHA` policies), previously orange.
  - `text-notice` — a non-status highlight (complimentary plan, private interconnect), previously purple.
  - `text-series-1` … `text-series-8` — palettes assigned by _position_ rather than meaning: log-stream labels, environment-diff sides. Eight distinct hues, not a severity ramp. Do not use a status token for a categorical slot, and do not half-migrate an array (a `["text-info", "text-fuchsia-400", …]` list is worse than either end).
  - Because the token adapts on its own, a `dark:text-*` companion is now redundant — delete it rather than porting it.
  - Alpha-tinted backgrounds and borders (`bg-red-500/10`, `border-amber-500/40`) were deliberately left as palette classes: they sit behind text rather than being it, and both schemes read them acceptably.
  - Known remaining gap: `--color-accent` is 4.17:1 on `surface-sunken` in light and 4.05:1 in dark, so it is not yet in the tested set.
  - The mobile app is _not_ affected — `mobile/src/lib/theme.ts` is a dark-only named-token object (`colors.danger`, `colors.success`, …) with no Tailwind palette classes, so there is nothing to mirror.
- **No status dots.** Problems are marked with `IssueIndicator` (`ui/src/components/IssueIndicator.tsx`): a warning triangle whose `aria-label` is the reason and whose hover tooltip (positioned with `@popperjs/core`, portalled to `body` or the nearest open `<dialog>`, Escape dismisses) shows it. `react-popper` is not used: it stops at React 18, `tone="danger"` or `"warning"`. Healthy, neutral, pending and connected states get no marker at all; a coloured dot carried no reason and was unreadable to colour-blind users. Plugin `status-dot` nodes still exist in the schema contract, but `StatusDotNodeRenderer`/`StatusIssueIndicator` only draw the triangle for `error` and `degraded` (via `statusIssueTone` in `schema-tokens.ts`), using the node's `label` as the tooltip. Mobile has a native `IssueIndicator` (`mobile/src/components/IssueIndicator.tsx`) that shows the reason on tap, since a phone has no hover. Small round markers that remain (picker selection indicators, Docker setup step progress, the settings "changed" marker) are not status and are deliberate.
- **Tables** — every `<th>` carries a `scope`. Column headers in a `<thead>` are `scope="col"`; the app has no row-header tables today, so a `scope="row"` means someone promoted a first-column `<td>` and should say why. A table gets an explicit accessible name **only when nothing adjacent already supplies one**: a `<caption className="sr-only">` where the table stands alone in a panel or a result pane whose only neighbours are a toolbar or a toggle button (query results, the file list, artifacts, secret versions, deploy history, the admin org list), and nothing at all where a visible heading sits immediately above it (`ChildResourceTable`'s `spec.title`, "Deploy on push", "Recent firings", "Lines", "Anomalies", every settings section) — a second announcement of a name the user just heard is noise, not help. Tables whose name is supplied from outside the component get neither: `ChatMarkdown` renders a model-authored table and `SchemaRenderer`'s `TableNode` has no label field. Several `<table>`s are pure row layout with no `<thead>` at all (DNS zones, savings, posture, expiry, the env-diff field lists); they need no `scope` and no caption.
- **Website landmarks** — `app/packages/website` is Astro and shares none of the above CSS. Every page wraps its content in `<main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">` (`index.astro`, `privacy.astro`, and `DocsLayout.astro` for everything under `/docs`), and `Nav.astro` — which is the first thing in `<body>` on every page — opens with `<a class="skip-link" href="#main-content">`. That single placement is what gives the skip link to the whole site; the docs layout is where it earns its keep, since the sidebar `<nav>` is ~60 links deep and precedes the article on every page. `.skip-link` lives in `src/styles/global.css` (offscreen via `transform`, revealed on focus, with a `prefers-reduced-motion` branch) — do not reach for the apps' Tailwind `sr-only`, which that package does not share. Markdown tables in the docs get their `scope="col"`/`scope="row"` from `src/lib/rehype-table-scope.mjs`, wired into `astro.config.mjs` beside `remarkDocs`, so authors never hand-write HTML to get a readable table.

## Code conventions from the July 2026 quality sweep

Nine parallel passes over the whole repo (deduplication, shared types, dead code, circular
imports, weak types, defensive code, legacy paths, comments, godfiles). The rules below are what
those passes established or discovered; the reasoning is preserved because in several places the
obvious-looking cleanup is the wrong one.

### Where a shared type lives

There is no `shared-types` package — do not create one. Types go in exactly one of four places,
chosen by who must agree:

- **`@infrawrench/plugin-base`** — the plugin↔host contract. Zero internal dependencies; nothing
  may make it depend on an app package.
- **`@infrawrench/client-core`** — every HTTP wire shape, plus the pure client logic that operates
  on it (cost contract, dashboard cards, chat, WS frames, push payloads, account-section rules).
  Depends only on `plugin-base`. This is the home for anything the _server produces and a client
  consumes_: `web`, `desktop`, `mobile`, `server-core` and the CLI all reach it.
- **`@infrawrench/ui`** — React-facing types (component props, editor state) plus a re-export shim
  over client-core, because web and desktop depend on `ui` rather than client-core directly.
  `ui/src/api-types.ts` is that shim: add new wire types to `client-core/src/api-types.ts`.
- **the owning package** — anything genuinely local.

`server-core` depends on `client-core`, never the reverse, so a wire contract is declared once and
the producer is typechecked against it. Annotate a route's service function with the client-core
type rather than letting the object literal float — `getOrgCostStatus` went unannotated while three
separate declarations claimed to describe its output.

Prefer deriving over restating: `z.infer`, `$inferSelect`, `Extract<Union, {…}>`, `Omit<…>`. Where
a zod schema and a hand-written type must match, pin them with the `Exact<A, B>` assertion pattern
in `ui/src/cost/config.ts` — it fails the build on drift and costs nothing at runtime.

**Mobile is the tell.** If a type lives in `ui` and mobile needs it, mobile _cannot_ import it and
will silently hand-write a second copy. That is how the mobile billing screen came to read
`GET /billing/status` as a bare subscription when the server returns a
`{ complimentary, subscription }` envelope — every org rendered blank plan rows for as long as both
copies existed.

### Module layering and circular imports

The workspace package graph is a DAG and should stay one: `plugin-base` and `client-core` are
leaves, `ui` depends on `client-core` and never the reverse, `server-core` depends on the plugins,
and `web`/`desktop`/`mobile`/`poller` sit on top. Adding an `@infrawrench/*` dependency that points
back down the stack is the one thing that turns a clean graph into a tangled one.

Check with `npx madge --circular --extensions ts,tsx --ts-config tsconfig.json src` from inside a
package (its own tsconfig, so `@/…` aliases resolve), or
`npx dpdm --no-warning --no-tree --exit-code circular:1 'src/**/*.ts'`, which additionally follows
pnpm workspace links. Neither is a devDependency; run them with `npx`.

Where a module has both a contract (types describing a payload) and machinery (DB queries, network
transport), put the contract in its own import-free leaf. `server-core/src/push/` is the pattern:
`types.ts` (leaf) ← `expo-client.ts` (transport) ← `dispatch.ts` (DB fan-out), with `dispatch.ts`
re-exporting the types so the published `push/dispatch` subpath stays stable. This matters more
than the cycle itself — `db/client` opens a connection as an import side effect, so a type living
beside it is a connection waiting to be opened by a consumer who only wanted a string union.

### Error handling

Errors must reach a place a human sees: an HTTP response, a WS error frame, a toast or React error
state, a structured log in a long-running process, or a non-zero CLI exit. A `catch` that returns
`[]`, `null` or `0` turns a backend outage into an empty UI, which is worse than a 500 because
nobody can tell it apart from "you have no data".

- **`isXConfigured()` and "X is broken" are different states.** ClickHouse readers
  (`server-core/src/clickhouse/readers.ts`) return `[]` when ClickHouse is not configured — that
  deployment genuinely has no metric history. A configured-but-failing ClickHouse throws.
- **`Promise.allSettled` is for isolation, not for ignoring.** Wherever it keeps one failure from
  killing a batch (poller type listings, pin probes, notification fan-out), the rejected `reason`
  must still be logged with enough context to identify which item failed.
- Fan-out helpers (`sendSlackToOrg`, `sendMsTeamsToOrg`, `sendPushToOrg`) deliberately return
  delivery counts instead of throwing, and each has a `…Test` counterpart that _does_ throw so the
  settings UI can show the real transport error. Keep that pairing when adding a transport.

### Shared write helpers in `server-core`

Three invariants that used to be copy-pasted now live in one place each:

- **`secret-states`** — `setLiteralSecretState` / `setOutputRefSecretState`. A
  `secret_field_states` row is either a literal or an output-ref, and writing one kind must clear
  the other kind's columns. Adding a column to that table means updating the clear-list in
  `src/secret-states.ts` and nowhere else. (The seven inlined copies had drifted: one flipped
  `resolution_kind` to `output-ref` while leaving `encrypted_value` populated, retaining secret
  material the user believed they had replaced.)
- **`created-resource`** — `upsertCreatedResource`, for the four flows that create a resource and
  need its `resources` row before the next sync. Deliberately distinct from `sync-resources`'s
  `upsertResource`, which merges JSON columns and bumps `sync_version` because a lister's view is
  partial; a create response is authoritative and overwrites.
- **`tick-loop`** — the `TickLoop` base class behind the poller and github-watcher, plus
  `runService` / `installShutdownHandlers`. Ticks are scheduled after the previous one settles,
  never on a fixed interval; an overrunning tick is skipped rather than run concurrently; `stop()`
  allows 30s of drain to match Kubernetes' `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.

`server-core/env-loader.mjs` is the single dev-time `.env` preloader for web, poller and
github-watcher. It searches `app/packages/web/` first (that package owns the canonical `.env`),
then the cwd, and never overwrites an existing `process.env` entry.

`@infrawrench/ui`'s `src/components/schema-tokens.ts` owns the mapping from a plugin's
`BadgeNode.color` / `StatusDotNode.status` to Tailwind classes. Renderers must not inline their own
ladder — the peer pane and the detail view previously drew `degraded` in two different yellows.

### Typing vendor SDK request bodies

Plugin clients assemble create/update bodies from a `Record<string, string>` of form fields.
Annotate the body with the SDK's own params type (`const body: XCreateParams = {…}`) — never build
a `Record<string, unknown>` and cast. The cast is not free: it hides the case where a free-text
form field is posted against a closed string-literal union, which is a silent API 400. Removing 36
such casts from the Cloudflare plugin surfaced 17 live wire-format bugs. When a form value must
become a literal union, narrow it with a membership guard and a documented default:

```ts
const METRICS = ["cosine", "euclidean", "dot-product"] as const;
type Metric = (typeof METRICS)[number];
const isMetric = (v: string): v is Metric => (METRICS as readonly string[]).includes(v);
```

A second cast is not a fix. If the params type is a discriminated union the body genuinely cannot
satisfy (Cloudflare DNS records, Page Rules actions), keep the cast and name the union and the
`.d.ts` line in a comment.

- **Hand-written ambient module declarations are unverified.** `.d.ts` files we author for untyped
  dependencies (e.g. `memcached/src/memjs.d.ts`) are asserted, not checked — a wrong signature
  there is worse than no types, because call sites work around it with casts instead of fixing it.
  That file promised a `stats(): Promise<…>` that memjs does not have. Read the dependency's source
  before declaring a method.
- **`tsc` (TypeScript 7 / native) historically did not surface mixin-provided members** (`class X extends Mixin(Base) {}`). mysql2's
  `query`/`execute` are the live example, so those casts are load-bearing — build the local
  interface out of the library's own exported packet types so a breaking upgrade still shows up.
- **`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`** is inherited by every package including `ui`. Widen the
  _declaration_ to `prop?: T | undefined` when the type is ours; use a conditional spread
  `{...(v !== undefined ? { k: v } : {})}` when the receiving type is a third party's.

### Dead-code tooling

`knip.json` drives the sweep (`npx knip`). Two things about it are load-bearing:

- **Entry points must match the real build inputs, not the obvious file.** The desktop main-process
  entry is `electron/index.ts` (the `--cli` dispatcher), _not_ `electron/main.ts`. Pointing knip at
  `main.ts` makes it report the entire `electron/cli/` tree — the shipped CLI — as dead code.
- **`@kubernetes/client-node`, `cloudflare`, `dockerode` and `ssh2` are deliberately direct
  dependencies** of `web`, `poller` and `github-watcher` even though no source file imports them.
  Each esbuild `build` script marks them `--external:`, so they must resolve from `node_modules` at
  runtime, reached through the plugin node drivers. They sit in `ignoreDependencies` — do not
  "clean them up".

Knip's `exports` and `types` buckets are noisy here: a type referenced only by an exported
signature in its own module still counts as unused. Treat that bucket as informational.

### TypeScript 7 + tsdown

TypeScript 7 ships the Go-native compiler as `tsc` (platform binaries under `@typescript/typescript-*`). The monorepo pins `typescript@^7.0.2` everywhere for typecheck/build.

Library packages build with **tsdown** (not tsup). tsup's DTS path still depends on the classic TS JS API and cannot run on pure TS 7; tsdown emits types via the native compiler and peers `typescript@^5 || ^6 || ^7`. Configs live in `tsdown.config.ts` and use `outExtensions` so output names stay `index.js` / `index.cjs` / `index.d.ts` / `index.d.cts` (matching the previous tsup layout). `unrun` is an optional peer used whenever Node lacks type stripping; keep it as a root `devDependency` so EAS (and any Node < 22.6) can still load those configs — see Mobile CI.

TS 7 does **not** ship a stable JS compiler API yet (expected in 7.1). The few places that still need `transpileModule` / `createProgram` / `ts.sys` import `@typescript/typescript6` explicitly (or alias `typescript` to it):

- `workflow-runtime` (runtime transpile + headless typecheck + `copy-ts-libs.mjs`)
- `web` SDK generator (`scripts/sdk/targets/typescript`)
- `website` keeps `typescript` aliased to `@typescript/typescript6` for `@astrojs/check` (peer is still `^5 || ^6`)
- `mobile` keeps the same alias: Expo CLI's `evaluateTsConfig` does `ts.sys.getCurrentDirectory` when Metro starts (`expo export:embed` on EAS), and pure TS 7 leaves `ts.sys` undefined — fails with `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'getCurrentDirectory')`. Bumping Expo does not help until it stops requiring the classic JS API.

`tsconfig.base.json` sets `types: ["*"]` (TS 6/7 default is `[]`). Do **not** reintroduce `@typescript/native-preview` / `tsgo` / tsup.

**`noUnusedLocals` is not enabled in any tsconfig**, so dead imports and locals are invisible to
`pnpm typecheck`. A periodic `tsc --noEmit --noUnusedLocals -p <pkg>/tsconfig.json` sweep is the
only thing that catches them; it found 123 where knip found one unused file in ~1,830.

### Decomposing big plugin clients

Split by vendor domain, not by line count. The established shape (AWS, and now DigitalOcean) is a
thin `PluginClient` class owning auth, caches and dispatch, delegating to ctx-object modules beside
it: `create-handlers.ts` (dispatcher) + `create-handlers/<domain>.ts`, `detail-renderers.ts`
(barrel) + `detail-renderers/<domain>.ts`, `resource-listers.ts`, `metric-series.ts`,
`enrich-detail.ts`, `status-dots.ts`, `nosql-console.ts`. Each extracted module takes a narrow
context interface holding just the `fetch` wrapper and the caches it needs, so modules stay
leaf-ward of the client and unit-test with a fake `fetch`. The original module path always keeps
exporting the same names, so a split is never a breaking change.

`create-handlers/` modules return `null` for a `typeId` they do not handle; the dispatcher takes
the first non-null result and throws if every module declines. Arms are mutually exclusive, so
module order is not significant.

A big file is not automatically a godfile. `cloudflare/src/metric-series.ts` is ~1,750 lines of one
export over 12 homogeneous per-product fetchers — splitting it buys a 13-import barrel and nothing
else. `desktop/src/lib/agent-client.ts` is multi-responsibility but knitted together by six
module-level singleton maps, where a wrong split is a silent duplicate-VM-provision bug.

### Legacy paths deliberately kept

- **`organization_members.role` / `invitations.role` text fallback.** Migration `0009` added
  `role_id` with no backfill; it is populated lazily by `backfillMembershipRole()`, so production
  still has `role_id IS NULL` rows where the text fallback is the only thing resolving permissions.
- **API-key legacy SHA-256 lookup / `legacyHashSunsetAt`** — an active self-terminating sunset, not
  stale compat. Removing it locks out keys still sitting in customers' CI.
- **The `{ role }` body param and the `resourceIds` reorder form** — superseded for first-party
  clients but published in `openapi.json` and all nine SDKs, so removal is a major bump.
- **v1 ciphertext reads, desktop `master.key`, GCP legacy Cloud Run ids, AWS `legacyHost()`** — all
  read data at rest or are the only implementation of a live path.

`APP_URL` is now the only app-origin env var; the `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL` fallback (a leftover from
the pre-Hono Next.js shell) is gone. `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` still takes precedence for the OpenAPI
server URL and the MCP well-known documents only. `invitations.token` was dropped in migration
`0035_concerned_mesmero` — invitations are hash-only at rest, the raw token existing only in the
one-time `POST /team/invitations` response. `decrypt()` now always takes an AAD; desktop's
`main-utils.ts` keeps `aad` optional because it still writes v1 for cloud tokens.

### Known-broken, recorded rather than fixed

- **Chat metered billing has no replay path.** `web/src/chat/billing.ts` reports each `chat_usage`
  row to Stripe best-effort. If Stripe is unreachable the row keeps a null `stripeUsageRecordId`
  and is never retried — that usage is not billed. `chat_usage_unreported_idx` exists to support a
  replay job that has not been written. Do not assume unreported rows are eventually reconciled.
- **Fallback rows must not invent field values.** When a lister's `Describe*` enrichment fails,
  push empty strings for the fields you could not read (see the ACM fallback in
  `aws/src/resource-listers-extended/security.ts`), never a plausible default. The WAF, Cognito and
  Step Function fallbacks in that file violate this and will display `defaultAction: ALLOW` /
  `mfaConfiguration: OFF` for resources whose real posture is unknown.
- **Mobile secret fields render a "Tap to copy" affordance wired to nothing** — the
  `resolveFieldValue` handler it dispatches to is supplied by no screen, so it silently no-ops.
- **`FilestoreInstanceResourceType`** is fully implemented in the GCP plugin — lister, create
  config, create, delete, resolve-output, tests — and simply never registered in the manifest.

## Weekly digest

The weekly org summary (spend WoW + movers, sync incidents, resource churn) lives in
`server-core/src/digest/`: `compose.ts` is pure (window math, schedule math, totals/movers, all
three transports' formatting — unit-tested without mocks in `__tests__/digest-compose.test.ts`),
`weekly.ts` does the gathering, claiming, delivery and retry bookkeeping, `narrative.ts` is the
optional LLM paragraph, `recipients.ts` the email address list. Scheduling is the poller's fourth
tick pass (`tickDigests` in `poller/src/loop.ts`). Exactly-once across replicas/restarts comes from
one conditional UPDATE on `org_digest_settings.last_sent_week_start` — only rows the UPDATE moved
forward are returned to send, and **that column never moves backwards**, which is what keeps the
invariant true across timezone changes (`GREATEST(...)` in the settings upsert enforces it).
Delivery reuses `sendSlackToOrg`/`sendMsTeamsToOrg` with the fifth channel trigger `weeklyDigest`
(`ChannelTrigger` in `push/types.ts` — deliberately _not_ a `PushTrigger`; the digest never goes to
mobile push), plus email. Sync incidents are counted from `paging_incidents`, not
`account_sync_failures` — the failure table is a rolling window the pager prunes within minutes and
skips entirely while paging is off, so it cannot answer "how many last week". Enabling the digest
stamps `last_sent_week_start` to the current window so the first scheduled send is the next send
time, not the moment the toggle flips.

**Per-org schedule and the week-boundary math** (migration `0053`). `org_digest_settings` gained
`timezone` (IANA, default `UTC`), `send_day` (ISO 1–7, default 1) and `send_hour` (0–23, default 7),
